bethany.name: Bethany
bethany.note: A village on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, about 2 miles (15 stadia, John 11:18) from Jerusalem, home of Martha, Mary and Lazarus. Today it is al-Eizariya, a name that comes from Lazarus. A rock-cut tomb honored as Lazarus's since at least the 4th century lies in the village.

bethsaida.name: Bethsaida (Julias)
bethsaida.note: A fishing village just east of where the Jordan enters the lake, in the territory of Philip the tetrarch. Josephus says Philip raised it to a city and named it Julias. John 1:44 calls it the town of Philip, Andrew and Peter. Two sites are excavated: et-Tell, about 1.5 miles inland, and el-Araj near the shore.

burqin.name: Between Samaria and Galilee (Burqin)
burqin.note: Luke 17:11 places the healing of the ten lepers on the border between Samaria and Galilee, as Jesus entered an unnamed village. Local Christian tradition places it at Burqin, near Jenin, where the old Church of St George is said to stand over a cave where the lepers lived.

caesareaphil.name: Caesarea Philippi
caesareaphil.note: A town at one of the main springs of the Jordan, at the foot of Mount Hermon. Philip the tetrarch rebuilt old Paneas and named it for Caesar and himself. Beside the spring were a cave and shrines to the god Pan, and Herod the Great had built a temple to Augustus there. Today it is Banias.

capernaum.name: Capernaum
capernaum.note: A fishing town on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee, on the road toward Damascus. It became Jesus' home base in Galilee (Matthew 9:1 calls it "his own city"). The white limestone synagogue of the 4th–5th century stands on the black basalt foundations of an earlier one, and a modern church hovers over the house honored as Peter's.

decapolis.name: Decapolis
decapolis.note: A league of about ten Greek cities, most of them east of the Jordan and the lake, such as Hippos, Gadara, Gerasa and Pella. The population was largely Gentile. Mark does not name the exact place where Jesus healed the deaf man or fed the four thousand.

ephraim.name: Ephraim (Taybeh)
ephraim.note: John 11:54 says Jesus withdrew to "a town called Ephraim" near the wilderness. It is usually identified with et-Taiyiba (Taybeh), on a hilltop about 4 miles northeast of Bethel looking down toward the Jordan Valley, the Ophrah of Joshua 18:23.

galilee.name: Towns and villages of Galilee
galilee.note: Lower Galilee, the hill country west of the Sea of Galilee ruled by Herod Antipas. It was dense with farming villages and small towns linked by roads. The point stands for Jesus' movements through the region rather than one place.

gennesaret.name: Plain of Gennesaret
gennesaret.note: A small, very fertile plain on the northwest shore, between Magdala and Capernaum. Josephus praised its mild climate and its walnut, palm, fig and olive trees.

hermon.name: Mount Hermon
hermon.note: The snow-capped mountain, about 9,200 ft high, that rises above Caesarea Philippi. Robertson and many other scholars place the Transfiguration on one of its slopes because the Gospels set the scene a week after Peter's confession near Caesarea Philippi. A tradition since the 4th century names Mount Tabor instead.

judeacountry.name: Judean countryside
judeacountry.note: John 3:22 says only that Jesus and his disciples went "into the land of Judea" and stayed there baptizing. No town is named. The point marks the Judean countryside outside Jerusalem, toward the Jordan.

magdala.name: Magdala (Magadan, Dalmanutha)
magdala.note: Matthew 15:39 names Magadan and Mark 8:10 "the district of Dalmanutha"; neither name is known from any other source. Many copyists changed Magadan to the familiar Magdala, the fishing town on the west shore that was the home of Mary Magdalene. Excavations there since 2009 have uncovered a 1st-century synagogue and the carved "Magdala stone."

olives.name: Mount of Olives
olives.note: The ridge east of Jerusalem across the Kidron Valley, about 2,700 ft high. Constantine built the Eleona church over a cave near the summit; the Pater Noster church there today recalls the teaching of the Lord's Prayer.

perea.name: Perea (beyond the Jordan)
perea.note: The land east of the Jordan from Pella south to Machaerus, ruled with Galilee by Herod Antipas. Galilean pilgrims often went down this side of the river to avoid Samaria, crossing back at Jericho. The Gospels name no Perean towns for this ministry.

samariavillage.name: A Samaritan village
samariavillage.note: Luke does not name the village. The direct road from Galilee to Jerusalem ran through Samaria, about a three-day walk; Ginae (modern Jenin), on the border where the Jezreel Valley meets the hills, was the first Samaritan town on it. Josephus tells of Galilean pilgrims being attacked there on the way to a feast.

seagalilee.name: Sea of Galilee (on the water)
seagalilee.note: A freshwater lake about 13 miles long and 8 wide, nearly 700 feet below sea level, ringed by hills. Winds funnel down through the valleys and can raise sudden, violent storms. Fishing boats of the period held a crew of four or five and some passengers.

siloam.name: Pool of Siloam
siloam.note: A pool at the south end of the City of David, fed by Hezekiah's tunnel from the Gihon spring. In 2004 workers repairing a sewer uncovered the stepped edge of a large Second Temple period pool, widely identified as the pool of John 9. A Byzantine church once marked the older, smaller pool nearby.

tyre.name: Region of Tyre and Sidon
tyre.note: The old Phoenician port cities on the coast, outside Jewish territory and outside Herod Antipas' rule. Tyre lies about 35 miles northwest of Capernaum, and Sidon about 22 miles farther north. People from this region had already come to hear Jesus (Mark 3:8).

events.title: The feeding of the five thousand
people: A boy with five loaves and two fish
About 5,000 men, besides women and children
events.summary: The Twelve return from their mission, and Jesus takes them by boat to a lonely place near Bethsaida to rest. The crowds run ahead around the shore. Jesus has compassion on them, "like sheep without a shepherd," and teaches them. Toward evening he takes five barley loaves and two fish, gives thanks, and the disciples feed about five thousand men; twelve baskets of pieces are left over. It is the only miracle, apart from the Resurrection, told in all four Gospels.
events.stay: A rest away from the crowds was the purpose of the trip; Jesus and the Twelve spent the day on the grassy hillside with the crowd.
events.journey: About 4 to 5 miles by boat across the north end of the lake; the crowds walked around the shore, about 8 to 10 miles.

scripture.text: As he landed he saw a great throng, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd; and he began to teach them many things.
"There is a lad here who has five barley loaves and two fish; but what are they among so many?"

Then he ordered the crowds to sit down on the grass; and taking the five loaves and the two fish he looked up to heaven, and blessed, and broke and gave the loaves to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up twelve baskets full of the broken pieces left over.

echoes.note: Elisha feeds a hundred men with twenty barley loaves, and some is left over.
God feeds Israel with manna in the wilderness.

art.title: Loaves and fishes mosaic, Church of the Multiplication
art.artist: Byzantine mosaicist (photographed by the Matson Photo Service)
art.medium: Stone mosaic floor; black-and-white photograph
art.location: Church of the Multiplication, Tabgha, Sea of Galilee (photo: Library of Congress)
art.description: A basket of loaves flanked by two fish, set in the floor before the altar, photographed soon after the mosaic was uncovered in the 1930s.
art.significance: The church at Tabgha marks the pilgrim tradition of the feeding of the five thousand; the pilgrim Egeria described a stone altar here in the late 4th century.
art.symbolism: Only four loaves are visible in the basket: the fifth, many suggest, is the Eucharistic bread on the altar above it.
art.impact: Now one of the best-known images of Christian art in the Holy Land, reproduced on countless souvenirs and pottery from Galilee.

art.title: The Miracle of the Loaves and Fishes
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Thousands sit in rows along the green terraces of a steep hillside above a valley, while the disciples carry baskets of bread down the lines.
art.significance: Shows the scale of the miracle: Mark 6:39–40 says the people sat down "in groups, by hundreds and by fifties" on the green grass.
art.symbolism: The ordered ranks recall Israel's camp in the wilderness, fed with manna; the baskets moving through the crowd point to the twelve baskets left over.
art.impact: One of Tissot's grandest panoramas, and a widely reproduced image of the feeding.

events.orderNote: Luke 9:10 sets the miracle near Bethsaida, which Robertson takes as Bethsaida Julias on the northeast shore; Mark 6:45 then sends the disciples "to Bethsaida," which Robertson thinks was a second, western Bethsaida near Capernaum (others read it as the same town). Pilgrim tradition since the 4th century has honored the miracle at Tabgha on the northwest shore, where the Church of the Multiplication stands.

Mt.text: And those who ate were about five thousand men, besides women and children.

Mk.text: Then he commanded them all to sit down by companies upon the green grass. So they sat down in groups, by hundreds and by fifties.

Lk.text: When the crowds learned it, they followed him; and he welcomed them and spoke to them of the kingdom of God, and cured those who had need of healing.

Jn.text: "There is a lad here who has five barley loaves and two fish; but what are they among so many?"

events.title: Jesus refuses to be made king
events.summary: After the meal the crowd hails Jesus as "the prophet who is to come" and wants to seize him and make him king. He makes the disciples get into the boat at once and sends the crowd away. Then he goes up into the hills alone to pray. He will not be the political Messiah they hoped for.
events.stay: Jesus spent the evening and much of the night alone on the hillside in prayer.

scripture.text: When the people saw the sign which he had done, they said, "This is indeed the prophet who is to come into the world!" Perceiving then that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, Jesus withdrew again to the hills by himself.
And after he had taken leave of them, he went up into the hills to pray.

echoes.note: Moses promises that God will raise up a prophet like him; the crowd thinks of this "prophet who is to come."

art.title: The People Seek Jesus to Make Him King
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Crowds clamber over the rocky hillside above the lake, searching for Jesus. The Sea of Galilee and the plain stretch out far below.
art.significance: Tissot traveled in Palestine in 1886–87 and again in 1889 to sketch landscapes, and the wide view of the lake comes from those studies.
art.symbolism: Jesus himself is absent from the picture: the crowd hunts for a king they cannot find.
art.impact: Part of Tissot's 350-scene Life of Christ, a sensation when first shown in Paris in 1894 and widely reproduced in Bibles.

art.title: Jesus Goes Up Alone onto a Mountain to Pray
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Jesus stands alone on a rocky summit under a starry night sky and a crescent moon, arms spread wide in prayer.
art.significance: Illustrates Matthew 14:23 and Mark 6:46: after sending the crowd away, he goes up alone to pray.
art.symbolism: The open arms and the empty dark around him show the solitude he sought after refusing a worldly crown.
art.impact: One of the most reproduced images of Tissot's series for its simple, striking composition.

Mt.text: And after he had dismissed the crowds, he went up into the hills by himself to pray. When evening came, he was there alone,

Mk.text: Immediately he made his disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side, to Bethsaida, while he dismissed the crowd.

Jn.text: Perceiving then that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, Jesus withdrew again to the hills by himself.

events.title: Jesus walks on the water
events.summary: The disciples row against a strong wind for hours. In the fourth watch of the night, between 3 and 6 a.m., Jesus comes to them walking on the sea, and they cry out in fear, thinking he is a ghost. He says, "Take heart, it is I." Matthew adds that Peter walks on the water toward him, begins to sink when he sees the wind, and is caught by Jesus' hand. When Jesus gets into the boat the wind stops, and they worship him as the Son of God.
events.journey: Jesus came out to the boat in the middle of the lake; John says they had rowed about three or four miles.

scripture.text: But immediately he spoke to them, saying, "Take heart, it is I; have no fear."

And Peter answered him, "Lord, if it is you, bid me come to you on the water." He said, "Come." So Peter got out of the boat and walked on the water and came to Jesus; but when he saw the wind, he was afraid, and beginning to sink he cried out, "Lord, save me." Jesus immediately reached out his hand and caught him, saying to him, "O man of little faith, why did you doubt?"
And those in the boat worshiped him, saying, "Truly you are the Son of God."

echoes.note: God alone "trampled the waves of the sea."
"It is I" (literally "I am") echoes the divine name revealed to Moses.

art.title: Jesus Walks on the Sea
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Jesus, glowing white against the night, walks barefoot toward the viewer across dark, rippling water under a crescent moon, his hands raised.
art.significance: Illustrates Matthew 14:25–27 from the disciples' point of view in the boat: a figure coming toward them across the waves.
art.symbolism: The ghostly halo of light explains why the disciples cried out in fear, thinking he was a ghost; the raised hands echo his words "Take heart, it is I."
art.impact: One of Tissot's most haunting images, a companion to his picture of Peter sinking.

art.title: Saint Peter Walks on the Sea
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Peter, sinking to his waist in the dark water, throws up his hands. Jesus, in white, stands on the waves and reaches out to him; the disciples watch from the boat by lantern light under the moon.
art.significance: Illustrates Matthew 14:30–31, the moment Peter begins to sink and cries, "Lord, save me."
art.symbolism: The glowing white figure of Christ against the black night stands for faith's anchor in the storm; Peter's raised hands are a picture of every desperate prayer.
art.impact: Tissot's night scenes on the lake are among the most dramatic of his Life of Christ series.

Mt.text: And Peter answered him, "Lord, if it is you, bid me come to you on the water." He said, "Come." So Peter got out of the boat and walked on the water and came to Jesus;

Mk.text: And he got into the boat with them and the wind ceased. And they were utterly astounded, for they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened.

Jn.text: Then they were glad to take him into the boat, and immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going.

events.title: Healings at Gennesaret
events.summary: The boat comes to land at Gennesaret, and people recognize Jesus at once. They carry the sick on mats to wherever they hear he is. In villages, cities and countryside they lay the sick in the market places and beg to touch even the fringe of his garment, and all who touch it are made well.
events.journey: About 3 to 4 miles across the water to the western shore.

scripture.text: and ran about the whole neighborhood and began to bring sick people on their pallets to any place where they heard he was. And wherever he came, in villages, cities, or country, they laid the sick in the market places, and besought him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment; and as many as touched it were made well.

echoes.note: The fringes (tassels) on the garment that every Israelite wore, which the sick reached out to touch.

art.title: In the Villages the Sick Were Presented to Him
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Jesus walks down a narrow stepped street under a stone arch. The sick, the old and mothers with children crowd the steps on both sides, and he bends to touch a man leaning on a staff.
art.significance: Matches Mark 6:56: "wherever he came, in villages, cities, or country, they laid the sick in the market places."
art.symbolism: The steep, enclosed street funnels every sufferer toward Christ; his stooping posture shows a healer who comes down to meet them.
art.impact: Tissot drew such streets from life in the old towns of Palestine, so the setting feels like a real village rather than an idealized one.

Mt.text: And when the men of that place recognized him, they sent round to all that region and brought to him all that were sick,

Mk.text: And when they got out of the boat, immediately the people recognized him, and ran about the whole neighborhood and began to bring sick people on their pallets to any place where they heard he was.

events.title: The Bread of Life discourse
events.summary: The crowd finds Jesus in Capernaum the next day, hoping for more bread. In the synagogue he tells them he is the bread of life come down from heaven, and that whoever eats his flesh and drinks his blood has eternal life. Many disciples find this a hard saying and stop following him. Jesus asks the Twelve whether they too will go, and Peter answers, "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life." Jesus warns that one of them is a devil, meaning Judas.
events.journey: About 3 miles along the shore from Gennesaret to Capernaum.

scripture.text: Jesus said to them, "I am the bread of life; he who comes to me shall not hunger, and he who believes in me shall never thirst.
So Jesus said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you have no life in you;

After this many of his disciples drew back and no longer went about with him. Jesus said to the twelve, "Will you also go away?" Simon Peter answered him, "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life;

echoes.note: "I will rain bread from heaven for you": the manna the crowd raises (John 6:31).

art.title: You Follow Me for the Miracles
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Jesus stands on a rocky, flowered slope above the lake and speaks to people who have just come ashore by boat to find him.
art.significance: Illustrates John 6:26: "you seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves."
art.symbolism: The boats pulled up below show how hard the crowd worked to reach him; his raised hands turn them from bread that perishes to the bread of life.
art.impact: One of the few images of the opening of the Bread of Life discourse, a scene painters rarely attempted.

events.orderNote: John 6:59 places the discourse in the synagogue at Capernaum. Robertson calls this the collapse of the Galilean campaign: from here the crowds fall away and Jesus turns to training the Twelve.

events.title: The tradition of the elders: what defiles
events.summary: Pharisees and scribes come from Jerusalem and complain that Jesus' disciples eat without the ritual washing of hands required by the tradition of the elders. Jesus answers with Isaiah's words about honoring God with the lips while the heart is far away, and shows how their tradition can set aside God's commandment to honor father and mother. Then he tells the crowd that nothing going into a person defiles him, but what comes out of the heart. Mark adds, "Thus he declared all foods clean."
events.stay: Robertson places this probably in Capernaum. John 7:1 notes that Jesus now stayed in Galilee, because the Judeans sought to kill him.

scripture.text: And he said to them, "Well did Isaiah prophesy of you hypocrites, as it is written, 'This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the precepts of men.'
there is nothing outside a man which by going into him can defile him; but the things which come out of a man are what defile him."
And he said, "What comes out of a man is what defiles a man. For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, fornication, theft, murder, adultery,

echoes.note: "This people draw near with their mouth and honor me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me."

art.title: The Pharisees Question Jesus
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: In a colonnaded court, Jesus stands with arm outstretched, answering a knot of bearded Pharisees and scribes in rich robes, while ordinary people sit on mats around them.
art.significance: A general scene of Jesus disputing with the Pharisees, fitting the challenge over the tradition of the elders in Mark 7 and Matthew 15.
art.symbolism: The plain white robe of Jesus stands out against the layered, ornate dress of the religious experts, echoing his point that what matters is the heart, not outward show.
art.impact: Tissot's crowded debate scenes helped generations of readers picture the arguments of the Gospels as real, public encounters.

Mt.text: Then the disciples came and said to him, "Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?" He answered, "Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted will be rooted up.

Mk.text: And he said to them, "Then are you also without understanding? Do you not see that whatever goes into a man from outside cannot defile him, since it enters, not his heart but his stomach, and so passes on?" (Thus he declared all foods clean.)

Jn.text: After this Jesus went about in Galilee; he would not go about in Judea, because the Jews sought to kill him.

events.title: The Syrophoenician woman's daughter
people: A Greek woman of Syrophoenician birth ("a Canaanite woman")
events.summary: Jesus withdraws to the region of Tyre and Sidon and tries to stay hidden in a house. A Gentile woman begs him to drive a demon out of her daughter. He tests her: it is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs. She answers that even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their master's table. Jesus praises her great faith, and her daughter is healed from a distance.
events.stay: Jesus stayed in a house in the region of Tyre and did not want anyone to know (Mark 7:24).
events.journey: About 35 to 40 miles northwest through the hills of Upper Galilee to the coast.

scripture.text: But she answered him, "Yes, Lord; yet even the dogs under the table eat the children's crumbs." And he said to her, "For this saying you may go your way; the demon has left your daughter."

She said, "Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their master's table." Then Jesus answered her, "O woman, great is your faith! Be it done for you as you desire." And her daughter was healed instantly.

echoes.note: Elijah is sent to a widow of Zarephath, near Sidon, and raises her son: Jesus himself cited it (Luke 4:26).

art.title: The Woman of Canaan at the Feet of Christ
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.description: The woman kneels with clasped hands before Jesus, who reaches toward her, while an older apostle presses forward to send her away. A Gentile city with a pyramid-like tower rises behind.
art.significance: Drouais, a 20-year-old pupil of Jacques-Louis David, won the Prix de Rome with this painting in 1784.
art.symbolism: The apostle's gesture of dismissal (Matthew 15:23: "Send her away") contrasts with Christ's open hand; the foreign architecture marks her as an outsider.
art.impact: A celebrated example of early Neoclassical painting. Drouais died in Rome only four years later, aged 24.

art.title: The Canaanite's Daughter
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Jesus stands beneath a stone arch and stretches out his hand toward a group of women in red robes and jeweled headdresses who kneel and plead behind a low wall.
art.significance: Illustrates Matthew 15:21–28. Tissot dressed the women in the costume he observed among local women of the region.
art.symbolism: The low wall between them stands for the barrier between Jew and Gentile that the woman's faith crosses.
art.impact: Shows the scene in a real Near Eastern street rather than a classical setting, in contrast to Drouais.

events.orderNote: Robertson notes it was once questioned whether Jesus actually left the land of Israel; Matthew's wording and the best text of Mark 7:31 ("through Sidon") show that he did. This is the only time the Gospels record him outside the Jewish homeland, apart from the flight to Egypt.

Mt.text: He answered, "I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel."

Mk.text: Now the woman was a Greek, a Syrophoenician by birth. And she begged him to cast the demon out of her daughter. And he said to her, "Let the children first be fed, for it is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs."

events.title: "Ephphatha": the deaf man in the Decapolis
people: A deaf man with a speech impediment
Crowds with the lame, blind and maimed
events.summary: Jesus goes north through Sidon and then around into the Decapolis, east of the lake. People bring him a deaf man who can hardly speak. Jesus takes him aside, puts his fingers in his ears, touches his tongue, looks up to heaven, sighs, and says "Ephphatha," Aramaic for "Be opened." Matthew tells of great crowds bringing the lame, blind and maimed to him on a mountain, and they glorify the God of Israel.
events.journey: A long loop of about 100 miles: north up the coast to Sidon, east across the hills toward Hermon, and south through Philip's territory into the Decapolis, keeping out of Herod Antipas' land.

scripture.text: And taking him aside from the multitude privately, he put his fingers into his ears, and he spat and touched his tongue; and looking up to heaven, he sighed, and said to him, "Ephphatha," that is, "Be opened." And his ears were opened, his tongue was released, and he spoke plainly.
And they were astonished beyond measure, saying, "He has done all things well; he even makes the deaf hear and the dumb speak."

echoes.note: "The ears of the deaf unstopped... and the tongue of the dumb sing for joy." Mark's rare Greek word for the man's speech defect (7:32) appears elsewhere only in the Greek of this verse.

art.title: Jesus Heals the Blind and Lame on the Mountain
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: On a wooded slope high above the lake, people lead the sick and lame up the path to Jesus, who lays his hands on a kneeling man while the disciples stand by.
art.significance: Illustrates Matthew 15:29–31, Matthew's account of this visit: great crowds bring the lame, maimed, blind and dumb to him on the mountain by the sea.
art.symbolism: The long line of people winding up from the shore shows how far the news had spread among the Gentile towns.
art.impact: Tissot's view from the eastern heights over the water reflects his own sketches made by the lake.

events.orderNote: Robertson stresses that each of the withdrawals keeps out of Herod Antipas' territory and goes into Gentile, Greek-speaking districts.

Mt.text: so that the throng wondered, when they saw the dumb speaking, the maimed whole, the lame walking, and the blind seeing; and they glorified the God of Israel.

Mk.text: and looking up to heaven, he sighed, and said to him, "Ephphatha," that is, "Be opened."

events.title: The feeding of the four thousand
people: About 4,000 people, besides women and children
events.summary: A great crowd has been with Jesus three days in a lonely place and has nothing left to eat. He has compassion on them, for some have come a long way. With seven loaves and a few small fish he feeds about four thousand, and seven large baskets of pieces are left. Many of this crowd were probably Gentiles of the Decapolis.
events.stay: The crowd stayed with Jesus for three days (Mark 8:2).

scripture.text: "I have compassion on the crowd, because they have been with me now three days, and have nothing to eat;

And he commanded the crowd to sit down on the ground; and he took the seven loaves, and having given thanks he broke them and gave them to his disciples to set before the people; and they set them before the crowd.
And they ate, and were satisfied; and they took up the broken pieces left over, seven baskets full.

art.title: The Miracle of the Loaves and Fishes
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.location: Scuola Grande di San Rocco, Venice (upper hall)
art.description: On a dark hillside Christ hands bread to a disciple while a youth holds a basket. Below, a crowd of men, women and children reclines and reaches for food under a stormy, glowing sky.
art.significance: Part of Tintoretto's vast cycle for the confraternity of San Rocco, which cared for the poor and sick. The painting does not specify which of the two feedings it shows; it stands here for the meal in the Decapolis.
art.symbolism: The ceiling cycle above shows God feeding Israel in the wilderness, so this picture of bread for a hungry crowd answers the manna overhead.
art.impact: The San Rocco cycle, painted over more than twenty years, is often called Venice's answer to the Sistine Chapel.

events.orderNote: Some scholars think this is a second telling of the feeding of the five thousand. Robertson rejects that: Mark and Matthew report both, and both report Jesus himself referring to the two feedings (Mark 8:19–20; Matthew 16:9–10). Some pilgrim traditions set it at Tabgha, but Mark's order places it in the Decapolis.

Mt.text: Those who ate were four thousand men, besides women and children.

Mk.text: "I have compassion on the crowd, because they have been with me now three days, and have nothing to eat; and if I send them away hungry to their homes, they will faint on the way; and some of them have come a long way."

events.title: The Pharisees and Sadducees demand a sign
events.summary: Jesus crosses by boat to Magadan (Mark: Dalmanutha) on the Galilean side. At once Pharisees, now joined by Sadducees, come to test him by asking for a sign from heaven. He sighs deeply and tells them they can read the sky for the weather but not the signs of the times. No sign will be given to this generation except the sign of Jonah. Then he leaves them.
events.journey: About 12 to 15 miles from the Decapolis hills down to the eastern shore and across the lake by boat.

scripture.text: He answered them, "When it is evening, you say, 'It will be fair weather; for the sky is red.' And in the morning, 'It will be stormy today, for the sky is red and threatening.' You know how to interpret the appearance of the sky, but you cannot interpret the signs of the times. An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign shall be given to it except the sign of Jonah." So he left them and departed.
And he sighed deeply in his spirit, and said, "Why does this generation seek a sign? Truly, I say to you, no sign shall be given to this generation."

echoes.note: Jonah three days in the belly of the fish, which Jesus elsewhere links to his own death and rising (Matthew 12:40).

art.title: The Pharisees and the Saduccees Come to Tempt Jesus
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Jesus sits with his disciples on a stone bench under a great spreading tree. A richly robed group of Pharisees and Sadducees stands before him, one with hands on hips.
art.significance: Illustrates Matthew 16:1, the first time the Gospel shows the two rival parties joining forces against Jesus.
art.symbolism: The calm, seated Christ, palm open, contrasts with the stiff, demanding posture of the questioners who want a sign.
art.impact: Tissot took care to dress the two groups differently, a sign of the archaeological detail he aimed for throughout the series.

art.credit: Photo: Hanay, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
art.title: The Magdala stone
art.medium: Carved limestone block
art.location: Found in the synagogue at Magdala; photographed on display at the site
art.description: A low, footed limestone block carved with arches, rosettes and other decoration, shown in a glass case.
art.significance: Found in 2009 in the 1st-century synagogue at Magdala, a town where Jesus may well have taught. One face bears one of the earliest known carvings of the Temple menorah.
art.symbolism: Scholars read its carvings as a miniature of the Jerusalem Temple, linking this lakeside synagogue with worship in Jerusalem.
art.impact: One of the most important finds for picturing the Galilean synagogues of Jesus' day.

events.orderNote: The site of Magadan and Dalmanutha is unknown. Robertson notes that early copyists changed it to the familiar Magdala; he also notes this is the first time the Sadducees appear with the Pharisees against Jesus.

Mt.text: An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign shall be given to it except the sign of Jonah." So he left them and departed.

Mk.text: And he sighed deeply in his spirit, and said, "Why does this generation seek a sign? Truly, I say to you, no sign shall be given to this generation."

events.title: The leaven of the Pharisees; the blind man of Bethsaida
events.summary: Crossing the lake, the disciples find they have only one loaf. Jesus warns them against the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod, and they think he means bread. He rebukes their dullness: have they forgotten the five thousand and the four thousand? At Bethsaida people bring him a blind man. Jesus leads him out of the village, spits on his eyes and lays hands on him; at first the man sees people "like trees, walking," and after a second touch he sees clearly. It is the only miracle in the Gospels done in two stages.
events.journey: About 8 miles by boat across the north end of the lake to Philip's territory.

scripture.text: And he cautioned them, saying, "Take heed, beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod."

And he took the blind man by the hand, and led him out of the village; and when he had spit on his eyes and laid his hands upon him, he asked him, "Do you see anything?" And he looked up and said, "I see men; but they look like trees, walking." Then again he laid his hands upon his eyes; and he looked intently and was restored, and saw everything clearly.

art.title: The Lake of Gennesaret near the Site of Bethsaida
art.medium: Pen and ink over graphite on paper
art.description: A pen sketch of the lake shore: rocks and reeds in the shallows, and a low hill with a few huts and trees rising behind.
art.significance: Tissot drew it on his travels in the 1880s to record the setting of Bethsaida, where Jesus led the blind man out of the village (Mark 8:23).
art.symbolism: The empty shore reminds us that Jesus, under Antipas' threat, was now working away from the crowds of Galilee.
art.impact: Tissot's landscape studies gave his Life of Christ its sense of real places; the site of Bethsaida is still debated today.

Mt.text: Then they understood that he did not tell them to beware of the leaven of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.

Mk.text: And he looked up and said, "I see men; but they look like trees, walking."

events.title: Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi
events.summary: In the villages of Caesarea Philippi, after praying alone, Jesus asks the disciples who people say he is: John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah or one of the prophets. Then he asks, "But who do you say that I am?" Peter answers, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Jesus calls him blessed, names him Peter, the rock on which he will build his Church, and gives him the keys of the kingdom of heaven. He tells them to tell no one that he is the Christ.
events.stay: Robertson thinks Jesus spent several months in the region of Caesarea Philippi, quietly teaching the Twelve.
events.journey: About 25 miles north up the Jordan Valley, past the Huleh basin, to the springs of the Jordan.

scripture.text: He said to them, "But who do you say that I am?" Simon Peter replied, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God."

And Jesus answered him, "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona! For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the powers of death shall not prevail against it.
I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven."

echoes.note: The key of the house of David given to the king's steward: "he shall open, and none shall shut."
Robertson notes that the imagery here (build, rock, anointed, the power of Sheol, an everlasting throne) all appears in this psalm of David's line.

art.title: Delivery of the Keys
art.medium: Fresco
art.description: Christ hands the keys to the kneeling Peter, surrounded by the apostles and contemporary onlookers, on a vast paved square before a domed temple flanked by triumphal arches.
art.significance: Part of the wall cycle commissioned by Pope Sixtus IV for his new chapel, decades before Michelangelo painted its ceiling.
art.symbolism: The gold and silver keys stand for the power to bind and loose in heaven and on earth (Matthew 16:19); the central temple stands for the Church built on Peter.
art.impact: A landmark of Renaissance perspective; the young Raphael, Perugino's pupil, echoed its design in his Marriage of the Virgin.

art.title: The Primacy of Saint Peter
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: The disciples sit together on a rocky ledge beside a path under olive trees. Peter stands among them, hand raised to his head, as Jesus speaks to him.
art.significance: Illustrates Matthew 16:18–19, where Jesus names Simon the rock and promises him the keys.
art.symbolism: Tissot sets the scene against a wall of bare rock, recalling the word-play on Peter (Petros) and rock (petra).
art.impact: A quiet, informal version of a scene that churches usually show with great ceremony.

Mt.text: And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the powers of death shall not prevail against it.

Mk.text: And he asked them, "But who do you say that I am?" Peter answered him, "You are the Christ."

Lk.text: And he said to them, "But who do you say that I am?" And Peter answered, "The Christ of God."

events.title: The first prediction of the Passion: "Get behind me, Satan"
events.summary: From this time Jesus begins to teach plainly that the Son of man must suffer many things, be rejected by the elders, chief priests and scribes, be killed, and rise on the third day. Peter takes him aside and rebukes him. Jesus turns and rebukes Peter: "Get behind me, Satan!" Then he calls the crowd and tells them that anyone who would follow him must deny himself and take up his cross.

scripture.text: From that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.
But he turned and said to Peter, "Get behind me, Satan! You are a hindrance to me; for you are not on the side of God, but of men."

And he called to him the multitude with his disciples, and said to them, "If any man would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. For whoever would save his life will lose it; and whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel's will save it.

echoes.note: The suffering servant who is rejected, bears the sins of many, and is vindicated.

art.title: Get Thee Behind Me, Satan
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: On a stony road through barren hills, Jesus turns sharply on Peter with both hands raised, while the other disciples look on in surprise.
art.significance: Illustrates Matthew 16:23 and Mark 8:33, Jesus' rebuke when Peter tries to talk him out of the cross.
art.symbolism: The road behind them leads on toward Jerusalem: Peter is literally standing in the way.
art.impact: One of the few paintings of this sharp moment, which artists usually passed over in favor of the giving of the keys.

Mt.text: And Peter took him and began to rebuke him, saying, "God forbid, Lord! This shall never happen to you."

Mk.text: And he said this plainly. And Peter took him, and began to rebuke him. But turning and seeing his disciples, he rebuked Peter, and said, "Get behind me, Satan! For you are not on the side of God, but of men."

Lk.text: And he said to all, "If any man would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me.

events.title: The Son of man coming in his kingdom
events.summary: Jesus warns that whoever is ashamed of him and his words, the Son of man will be ashamed of when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels. He adds that some standing there will not taste death before they see the kingdom of God come with power. Each of the three Gospels places the Transfiguration immediately after this saying.

scripture.text: For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him will the Son of man also be ashamed, when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels."
And he said to them, "Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death before they see the kingdom of God come with power."

echoes.note: One like a son of man comes with the clouds and receives everlasting dominion.

art.title: Banias, ancient Caesarea Philippi
art.artist: Unknown photographer (lantern slide, Oregon State University Special Collections)
art.medium: Glass lantern slide
art.location: Oregon State University Special Collections & Archives
art.description: A traveler and a local guide look down from a spur of Mount Hermon over the stone houses and orchards of Banias and the plain beyond.
art.significance: Banias is the site of Caesarea Philippi, where Jesus gave these sayings about the cross and the coming kingdom.
art.symbolism: The view from the slopes of Hermon looks toward the spring-fed town and the land of Israel stretching south.
art.impact: Lantern slides like this one brought the landscapes of the Bible to church halls and lecture rooms in the early 20th century.

events.orderNote: Interpreters differ on what Jesus meant by the kingdom coming "with power" within that generation: the Transfiguration that follows, the Resurrection and Pentecost, or the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70.

Mt.text: For the Son of man is to come with his angels in the glory of his Father, and then he will repay every man for what he has done.

Mk.text: And he said to them, "Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death before they see the kingdom of God come with power."

Lk.text: For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of man be ashamed when he comes in his glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels.

events.title: The Transfiguration
events.summary: Six days later (Luke: about eight) Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain to pray. His face shines like the sun and his clothes become dazzling white. Moses and Elijah appear and speak with him about his "departure" (exodus) that he is to accomplish at Jerusalem. Peter offers to build three booths. A bright cloud overshadows them, and a voice says, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him." When they look up, they see only Jesus.
events.stay: Luke implies they spent the night on the mountain: the disciples were heavy with sleep, and they came down "on the next day" (Luke 9:32, 37).
events.journey: A climb from Caesarea Philippi onto the slopes of Mount Hermon, which rises directly above the town; the summit is about 12 to 14 miles away.

scripture.text: And after six days Jesus took with him Peter and James and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain apart. And he was transfigured before them, and his face shone like the sun, and his garments became white as light.
And behold, two men talked with him, Moses and Elijah, who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was to accomplish at Jerusalem.
He was still speaking, when lo, a bright cloud overshadowed them, and a voice from the cloud said, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him."

echoes.note: Moses on Sinai in the cloud of glory, his face shining when he came down.
"Him you shall heed": the voice's "listen to him" points to the prophet like Moses.

art.title: The Transfiguration
art.medium: Oil on panel
art.description: Above, Christ floats in a blaze of light between Moses and Elijah, while Peter, James and John fall dazzled on the mountaintop. Below, the other disciples are helpless before the possessed boy, whose family points upward to Christ.
art.significance: Raphael's last painting, nearly finished when he died in 1520 at the age of 37; it was hung above his body as he lay in state.
art.symbolism: The two halves join the Transfiguration with the next day's healing (Matthew 17:14–18): glory above, human need and failure below, and the boy's upturned eyes link the two.
art.impact: For centuries it was often called the greatest painting in the world. Napoleon carried it to Paris in 1797; it returned to Rome in 1816.

art.title: Transfiguration
art.medium: Oil on panel
art.description: Christ stands calmly in white on a low hilltop between Moses and Elijah, while Peter, James and John crouch or sit startled at their feet. A wide Italian countryside of farms and towns stretches behind.
art.significance: A late masterpiece of the Venetian master. Bellini sets the event in broad daylight on an ordinary hill rather than in a blaze of heavenly glory.
art.symbolism: The fence and rocky ledge in the foreground mark the mountain as holy ground set apart; the farmers and ox in the distance carry on, unaware.
art.impact: Its natural light and atmosphere were a turning point for Venetian landscape painting, opening the way for Giorgione and Titian.

events.orderNote: The Gospels say only "a high mountain." A tradition from the 4th century (Cyril of Jerusalem, Jerome) names Mount Tabor, where basilicas stand today; Robertson calls that tradition "beyond question false," since Tabor lies far to the south, in Galilee. He prefers a spur of Hermon; others suggest Mount Meron.

Mt.text: When the disciples heard this, they fell on their faces, and were filled with awe. But Jesus came and touched them, saying, "Rise, and have no fear."

Mk.text: and his garments became glistening, intensely white, as no fuller on earth could bleach them.

Lk.text: who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was to accomplish at Jerusalem.

events.title: Coming down the mountain: Elijah has come
events.summary: On the way down, Jesus tells the three to tell no one what they have seen until the Son of man is raised from the dead. They puzzle over what rising from the dead means, and ask why the scribes say Elijah must come first. Jesus answers that Elijah has already come and they did to him whatever they pleased, and so the Son of man will suffer at their hands. The disciples understand he is speaking of John the Baptist.

scripture.text: And as they were coming down the mountain, he charged them to tell no one what they had seen, until the Son of man should have risen from the dead.

but I tell you that Elijah has already come, and they did not know him, but did to him whatever they pleased. So also the Son of man will suffer at their hands." Then the disciples understood that he was speaking to them of John the Baptist.

echoes.note: "I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes."

art.title: The Transfiguration
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Christ, robed in brilliant white, rises in a burst of light above the mountaintop, with Moses and Elijah on either side and the three disciples cowering below.
art.significance: The vision the three disciples were ordered to keep secret "until the Son of man should have risen from the dead" (Mark 9:9).
art.symbolism: Elijah's presence in the vision is the key to the disciples' question on the way down: the Elijah who was to come had already come, in John the Baptist.
art.impact: Tissot renders the glory almost as pure light, a striking contrast to the earthy realism of most of his series.

art.title: Snow-clad Hermon from the Pharpar
art.medium: Glass negative
art.description: Snow-covered Mount Hermon rises on the horizon beyond a river meadow, with donkeys grazing by the water.
art.significance: Shows the long snowy ridge that Robertson and many others think was the "high mountain" of the Transfiguration.
art.symbolism: Hermon's snows feed the springs of the Jordan; in Psalm 133 its dew is a picture of God's blessing.
art.impact: Part of the Matson Collection, thousands of photographs of the Holy Land taken in the first half of the 20th century.

Mt.text: Then the disciples understood that he was speaking to them of John the Baptist.

Mk.text: So they kept the matter to themselves, questioning what the rising from the dead meant.

Lk.text: And when the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. And they kept silence and told no one in those days anything of what they had seen.

events.title: The boy the disciples could not heal
events.summary: At the foot of the mountain Jesus finds the other disciples arguing with scribes. A father has brought his only son, who is thrown into fits by a spirit, and the disciples could not cast it out. The father cries, "I believe; help my unbelief!" Jesus rebukes the spirit, and the boy lies like a corpse until Jesus takes his hand and lifts him up. Privately he tells the disciples that this kind can be driven out only by prayer and fasting, and that faith as small as a mustard seed could move mountains.
events.journey: Back down from the mountain to the villages around Caesarea Philippi, the next day.

scripture.text: And Jesus said to him, "If you can! All things are possible to him who believes." Immediately the father of the child cried out and said, "I believe; help my unbelief!"
And he said to them, "This kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer and fasting."

He said to them, "Because of your little faith. For truly, I say to you, if you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, 'Move from hence to yonder place,' and it will move; and nothing will be impossible to you."

art.title: Le possédé au pied du Thabor (The Possessed Boy at the Foot of Mount Tabor)
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: The boy lies twisted on his back on the hillside, mouth open, as his father kneels behind him. Jesus stands over them, one hand raised, while villagers watch from a town in the valley.
art.significance: Illustrates Mark 9:20–27. Tissot followed the old tradition that set the Transfiguration on Mount Tabor, so he placed this scene at its foot.
art.symbolism: Jesus' calm, upright figure in white contrasts with the boy's convulsed body and the anxious faces of the crowd.
art.impact: Brings out the raw physical drama of the healing that Raphael set beneath his Transfiguration.

Mt.text: He said to them, "Because of your little faith. For truly, I say to you, if you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, 'Move from hence to yonder place,' and it will move; and nothing will be impossible to you."

Mk.text: Immediately the father of the child cried out and said, "I believe; help my unbelief!"

Lk.text: While he was coming, the demon tore him and convulsed him. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, and healed the boy, and gave him back to his father.

events.title: The second prediction of the Passion
events.summary: Jesus passes through Galilee and does not want anyone to know, because he is teaching his disciples. He tells them again that the Son of man will be delivered into the hands of men, who will kill him, and that he will rise on the third day. They do not understand, and are afraid to ask him. Matthew says they were greatly distressed.
events.journey: About 30 to 35 miles south from Caesarea Philippi down the Jordan Valley into Galilee, traveling privately.

scripture.text: for he was teaching his disciples, saying to them, "The Son of man will be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him; and when he is killed, after three days he will rise."

"Let these words sink into your ears; for the Son of man is to be delivered into the hands of men." But they did not understand this saying, and it was concealed from them, that they should not perceive it; and they were afraid to ask him about this saying.

art.title: Jesus Discourses with His Disciples
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Jesus walks along a rocky valley road, deep in conversation with a disciple, while the others follow in small groups up the winding path.
art.significance: Matches Mark 9:30–31: they passed through Galilee and he did not want anyone to know, "for he was teaching his disciples."
art.symbolism: The quiet road away from the crowds shows the private training of the Twelve that marks this whole period.
art.impact: Tissot's scenes of Jesus on the road give a sense of how much of the Gospels' teaching happened on foot.

events.orderNote: Robertson ends the season of retirement from Galilee here (§§72–88), about six months from spring to autumn, and thinks the events of §§89–96 took only a few days.

Mt.text: As they were gathering in Galilee, Jesus said to them, "The Son of man is to be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him, and he will be raised on the third day." And they were greatly distressed.

Mk.text: But they did not understand the saying, and they were afraid to ask him.

Lk.text: "Let these words sink into your ears; for the Son of man is to be delivered into the hands of men."

events.title: The Temple tax and the coin in the fish
people: The collectors of the half-shekel tax
events.summary: Back in Capernaum, the collectors of the half-shekel Temple tax ask Peter whether his teacher pays it. Jesus asks Peter whether kings take tribute from their own sons or from others: the sons are free. Yet so as not to give offense, he sends Peter to cast a hook into the lake. In the mouth of the first fish he will find a shekel, enough to pay for both of them.
events.journey: About 10 to 15 miles back to Capernaum.

scripture.text: When they came to Capernaum, the collectors of the half-shekel tax went up to Peter and said, "Does not your teacher pay the tax?"

However, not to give offense to them, go to the sea and cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up, and when you open its mouth you will find a shekel; take that and give it to them for me and for yourself."

echoes.note: Every Israelite man was to pay half a shekel as an offering for the sanctuary.

art.title: The Tribute Money
art.medium: Fresco
art.location: Brancacci Chapel, Santa Maria del Carmine, Florence
art.description: Three moments in one scene: in the center the tax collector confronts Jesus and the apostles; at left Peter kneels by the lake to take the coin from the fish's mouth; at right he pays the collector.
art.significance: Painted for the Brancacci family's chapel of Saint Peter. It is the main painting of Matthew 17:24–27 in Western art.
art.symbolism: The circle of apostles around Christ suggests the Church gathered around him; Peter's two appearances show his obedience to Jesus' word.
art.impact: A founding work of Renaissance painting, with solid, sculptural figures, consistent light and perspective. Michelangelo studied and copied these frescoes as a young man.

events.title: Who is the greatest? A little child
events.summary: In the house at Capernaum Jesus asks the disciples what they were arguing about on the road. They are silent, for they had argued about who was the greatest. He sits down and tells them that whoever would be first must be last of all and servant of all. Then he puts a child in their midst, takes it in his arms, and says that whoever receives such a child in his name receives him.
events.stay: Jesus was in "the house" in Capernaum (Mark 9:33), probably Peter's home.

scripture.text: And he sat down and called the twelve; and he said to them, "If any one would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all."

and said, "Truly, I say to you, unless you turn and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever humbles himself like this child, he is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven.

And he took a child, and put him in the midst of them; and taking him in his arms, he said to them, "Whoever receives one such child in my name receives me; and whoever receives me, receives not me but him who sent me."

art.title: Jesus and the Little Child
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Jesus sits on stone steps in a town courtyard, holding a child close in his arms. The disciples stand before him in a silent, chastened row.
art.significance: Illustrates Mark 9:36: "taking him in his arms, he said to them..."
art.symbolism: The disciples, who had argued about greatness, stand while a child rests in the place of honor.
art.impact: A tender image often used in children's Bibles and catechisms.

Mt.text: and said, "Truly, I say to you, unless you turn and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.

Mk.text: And they came to Capernaum; and when he was in the house he asked them, "What were you discussing on the way?" But they were silent; for on the way they had discussed with one another who was the greatest.

Lk.text: and said to them, "Whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me; for he who is least among you all is the one who is great."

events.title: "He that is not against us"; the little ones and the lost sheep
events.summary: John tells Jesus they stopped a man casting out demons in his name because he was not one of them. Jesus says not to forbid him: whoever is not against us is for us, and even a cup of water given in his name will be rewarded. He warns against causing one of these little ones to sin: better a millstone around the neck. In Matthew he tells of the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to look for one lost sheep, for it is not the Father's will that one of these little ones should perish.

scripture.text: John said to him, "Teacher, we saw a man casting out demons in your name, and we forbade him, because he was not following us." But Jesus said, "Do not forbid him; for no one who does a mighty work in my name will be able soon after to speak evil of me. For he that is not against us is for us.
but whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to sin, it would be better for him to have a great millstone fastened round his neck and to be drowned in the depth of the sea.

What do you think? If a man has a hundred sheep, and one of them has gone astray, does he not leave the ninety-nine on the hills and go in search of the one that went astray? And if he finds it, truly, I say to you, he rejoices over it more than over the ninety-nine that never went astray. So it is not the will of my Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish.

echoes.note: Joshua wants Moses to stop Eldad and Medad prophesying in the camp; Moses answers, "Would that all the Lord's people were prophets."
God himself will seek out his lost sheep.

art.title: The Lost Sheep
art.artist: John Everett Millais (engraved by the Dalziel Brothers)
art.medium: Wood engraving
art.location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (this impression)
art.description: A shepherd struggles up a steep, rocky hillside with the lost sheep slung across his shoulders, while a bird of prey circles overhead.
art.significance: From Millais' The Parables of Our Lord, twenty wood engravings made over several years and counted among the finest Victorian book illustrations.
art.symbolism: The bird of prey shows the danger the sheep was in; the shepherd's bent back shows the cost of the search.
art.impact: Millais, a founder of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, set the parable in a real, rugged landscape rather than an idealized one.

events.orderNote: Luke tells the parable of the lost sheep again, more fully, to Pharisees and scribes later in the ministry (Luke 15:3–7). Robertson treats them as two occasions.

Mt.text: "See that you do not despise one of these little ones; for I tell you that in heaven their angels always behold the face of my Father who is in heaven.

Mk.text: But Jesus said, "Do not forbid him; for no one who does a mighty work in my name will be able soon after to speak evil of me. For he that is not against us is for us.

Lk.text: But Jesus said to him, "Do not forbid him; for he that is not against you is for you."

events.title: Forgiving a brother: the parable of the unmerciful servant
events.summary: Jesus teaches how to correct a brother who sins: first alone, then with witnesses, then before the Church. Where two or three are gathered in his name, he is among them. Peter asks whether he should forgive as many as seven times, and Jesus answers, "seventy times seven." He tells of a servant forgiven a debt of ten thousand talents who then throttles a fellow servant over a hundred denarii. The king hands him over to the jailers, "so also my heavenly Father will do to every one of you, if you do not forgive your brother from your heart."

scripture.text: For where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them."

Then Peter came up and said to him, "Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? As many as seven times?" Jesus said to him, "I do not say to you seven times, but seventy times seven.
Then his lord summoned him and said to him, 'You wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt because you besought me; and should not you have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?'

echoes.note: Lamech's boast of vengeance "seventy-sevenfold," which Jesus turns into a measure of forgiveness.

art.title: Parable of the Unforgiving Servant
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.description: A crowned king, chin in hand, sits at a table of ledgers and gold coins, pointing at an old man in debt who is held by two young attendants.
art.significance: Long known as "Croesus Receiving Tribute from a Lydian Peasant," it is now identified as the king of Jesus' parable settling accounts with his servants (Matthew 18:23–25).
art.symbolism: The scattered coins and the open account books recall the vast debt; the king's thoughtful gesture hints at the mercy to come.
art.impact: A showpiece of Vignon's rich, colorful style, which blended the influence of Caravaggio with the Venetian painters.

events.orderNote: Robertson's note puts the gap in modern terms: the king forgave about a million, and the servant would not forgive about ten. A talent was worth about 6,000 denarii, a laborer's wage for nearly 20 years.

events.title: The cost of following Jesus
events.summary: A scribe offers to follow Jesus wherever he goes. Jesus answers that foxes have holes and birds have nests, but the Son of man has nowhere to lay his head. To one who wants first to bury his father, he says, "Leave the dead to bury their own dead." To another who wants first to say farewell at home, he says that no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.

scripture.text: And Jesus said to him, "Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man has nowhere to lay his head."

To another he said, "Follow me." But he said, "Lord, let me first go and bury my father." But he said to him, "Leave the dead to bury their own dead; but as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God."
Jesus said to him, "No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God."

echoes.note: Elisha leaves his plow and his oxen to follow Elijah, after first saying farewell to his parents.

art.title: The Man at the Plough
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: An old farmer guides a wooden plow pulled by an ox and a donkey across a stony hillside field, looking back over his shoulder.
art.significance: Illustrates Luke 9:62: "No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God."
art.symbolism: The plowman's backward glance, while his furrow runs crooked, is the very image Jesus used for divided loyalty.
art.impact: Tissot painted the light plows and mixed teams he saw in use in Palestine in the 1880s.

events.orderNote: Matthew sets these sayings early, before the crossing to the Gadarenes; Luke sets them on the road after the Samaritan village. Robertson places them here, just before Jesus leaves Galilee, and notes that such sayings may have been repeated.

Mt.text: And a scribe came up and said to him, "Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go."

Lk.text: Another said, "I will follow you, Lord; but let me first say farewell to those at my home." Jesus said to him, "No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God."

events.title: The unbelieving brothers of Jesus
events.summary: The Feast of Tabernacles is near. Jesus' brothers urge him to go up to Judea and show his works to the world, for no one works in secret if he wants to be known. John explains that even his brothers did not believe in him. Jesus answers that his time has not yet come, though their time is always here, and he stays in Galilee.
events.stay: Jesus remained in Galilee for a few more days while his brothers went up to the feast (John 7:9).

scripture.text: So his brethren said to him, "Leave here and go to Judea, that your disciples may see the works you are doing. For no man works in secret if he seeks to be known openly. If you do these things, show yourself to the world." For even his brethren did not believe in him.
Jesus said to them, "My time has not yet come, but your time is always here.

art.title: Jesus Traveling
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Jesus walks with a few disciples across a wide, stony hillside, while families with donkeys travel in small groups along the slope behind them.
art.significance: The caravans of pilgrims suggest the crowds going up to the feasts at Jerusalem, as Jesus' brothers did at Tabernacles (John 7:10).
art.symbolism: Jesus stands a little apart from the flow of travelers: his time, he told his brothers, had not yet come.
art.impact: Tissot's wide landscapes from his trips to Palestine give the long walks of the Gospels their real scale.

events.orderNote: Who the "brothers" were is debated: Catholic and Orthodox tradition holds they were cousins or Joseph's sons by an earlier marriage; many Protestants take them as later children of Mary and Joseph. James, one of them, later led the church in Jerusalem.

events.title: Rejected by a Samaritan village
events.summary: When the days drew near for him to be received up, Jesus sets his face to go to Jerusalem. After his brothers have gone up to the feast, he goes too, privately, by the road through Samaria. He sends messengers ahead, but a Samaritan village will not receive him because he is going to Jerusalem. James and John offer to call down fire from heaven to consume them. Jesus turns and rebukes them, and they go on to another village.
events.journey: About 45 miles south from Capernaum through the Jezreel Valley to the edge of Samaria; Jerusalem lay about 70 miles farther, some three days on foot.

scripture.text: When the days drew near for him to be received up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem.

but the people would not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem. And when his disciples James and John saw it, they said, "Lord, do you want us to bid fire come down from heaven and consume them?" But he turned and rebuked them.

echoes.note: Elijah calls down fire from heaven on the king's soldiers, the precedent James and John have in mind.

art.title: He Went Through the Villages on the Way to Jerusalem
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Jesus and his followers climb toward a hill town of stone houses and palm trees, as villagers come out or sit and watch by the road.
art.significance: Tissot made it for Luke's long account of the journey to Jerusalem, which begins at Luke 9:51 with Jesus setting his face toward the city.
art.symbolism: The road climbing toward the town suggests the long ascent to Jerusalem that Luke describes.
art.impact: Shows the kind of hill village, packed with flat-roofed houses, where Jesus' messengers sought lodging.

events.orderNote: Luke 9:51 opens his long travel narrative (9:51–19:27). Robertson, joining Luke and John, takes this first journey as the secret one to the Feast of Tabernacles in John 7:10, not the final journey to the Passover; others read Luke's whole section as the last journey.

Lk.text: And when his disciples James and John saw it, they said, "Lord, do you want us to bid fire come down from heaven and consume them?" But he turned and rebuked them.

Jn.text: But after his brethren had gone up to the feast, then he also went up, not publicly but in private.

events.title: At the Feast of Tabernacles
events.summary: Jesus arrives in the middle of the week-long feast and teaches openly in the Temple. The crowds argue over whether he is a good man, a deceiver, or the Christ. On the last and greatest day he cries out that whoever thirsts should come to him and drink. Officers sent to arrest him come back empty-handed, and Nicodemus reminds the council that the Law does not condemn a man without a hearing.
events.stay: Pilgrims lived for the week of the feast in booths of branches in and around Jerusalem.
events.journey: About 45 to 50 miles, some three days on foot, by the ridge road through Samaria past Sychar and Bethel.

scripture.text: On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and proclaimed, "If any one thirst, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, as the scripture has said, 'Out of his heart shall flow rivers of living water.'"
The officers answered, "No man ever spoke like this man!"

echoes.note: The nations going up year by year to keep the feast of booths.
"With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation", a verse linked with the feast's daily water rite.

art.title: Reconstruction of Jerusalem and the Temple of Herod
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: A bird's-eye view of Jerusalem from the east: Herod's Temple with its vast colonnaded courts rises above the city wall, smoke climbing from the altar, with pilgrims and flocks on the slope below.
art.significance: Tissot made this reconstruction for his Life of Christ after studying the site and the archaeology of his day, to show the setting of Jesus' Temple teaching.
art.symbolism: The smoke of sacrifice at the heart of the city recalls that the great feasts brought all Israel up to the Temple.
art.impact: Helps the reader picture the scale of the courts where crowds argued about Jesus during the feast.

art.title: But No Man Laid Hands Upon Him
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Jesus, in white, teaches a seated crowd in a Temple colonnade while armed officers lean on the low wall nearby, watching but not moving.
art.significance: Illustrates John 7:30–46, where the officers sent to arrest Jesus return without him.
art.symbolism: The officers sit idle, weapons at rest: no one can touch Jesus before "his hour" has come.
art.impact: Shows how openly Jesus taught at the feast, under the eyes of those sent to seize him.

events.orderNote: Robertson dates this Tabernacles to October AD 29, six months before the crucifixion. The water-pouring and lamp-lighting rites of the feast, which John's sayings about living water and light seem to echo, are known from the Mishnah (Sukkah 4–5), written down about AD 200.

events.title: The woman caught in adultery
events.summary: Early in the morning Jesus comes from the Mount of Olives to teach in the Temple. Scribes and Pharisees bring a woman caught in adultery and ask whether she should be stoned, as Moses commanded, hoping to trap him. Jesus bends down and writes on the ground, then says that the one without sin should throw the first stone. They leave one by one, and he sends her away: "Go, and do not sin again."
events.stay: He spent the night on the Mount of Olives and came back to the Temple at dawn.

scripture.text: And as they continued to ask him, he stood up and said to them, "Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her."
Jesus looked up and said to her, "Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you?" She said, "No one, Lord." And Jesus said, "Neither do I condemn you; go, and do not sin again."

echoes.note: The Law's death penalty for adultery, for both the man and the woman.

art.title: The Woman Taken in Adultery
art.medium: Oil on oak panel
art.description: In a towering, shadowy Temple interior, a shaft of light falls on the kneeling woman in white and on the tall, calm figure of Christ, while her accusers crowd around. A golden high altar glitters in the gloom behind.
art.significance: One of Rembrandt's finest small history paintings, painted with the care of a miniature.
art.symbolism: The light picks out only the woman and Christ: mercy and the sinner meet, while the accusers stay in half-shadow.
art.impact: A treasured work of the National Gallery's Dutch collection and an often-reproduced image of this scene.

art.title: Christ and the Woman Taken in Adultery
art.medium: Oil on panel (grisaille)
art.description: Painted in shades of grey, Christ kneels and writes on the ground while the woman stands quietly behind him and the scribes and Pharisees lean in to read.
art.significance: A rare small grisaille, apparently painted for Bruegel's own circle rather than for sale; it was copied many times, including in an engraving of 1579.
art.symbolism: The words Christ writes are legible, in Dutch: "He that is without sin...". Painted in years of religious persecution in the Netherlands, it is often read as a plea for mercy and tolerance.
art.impact: One of the most admired works of the Courtauld collection, and an unusual image that shows the moment of writing rather than the woman's shame.

events.orderNote: Most of the oldest manuscripts do not have this passage, and some place it elsewhere (after John 7:36 or Luke 21:38). Robertson thinks it is very probably a true story of Jesus, perhaps preserved by Papias, and notes that without it John 8:12 follows straight on from John 7:52. The Catholic Church receives it as canonical Scripture.

events.title: "I am the light of the world"
events.summary: Speaking in the treasury of the Temple, Jesus declares that he is the light of the world. The Pharisees object that he bears witness to himself. He answers that the Father who sent him bears witness too. No one arrests him, "because his hour had not yet come."

scripture.text: Again Jesus spoke to them, saying, "I am the light of the world; he who follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life."

echoes.note: The Servant given "as a light to the nations."
The pillar of fire that gave Israel light in the wilderness.

art.title: Jesus Speaks Near the Treasury
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Jesus, seen from behind in a white mantle, sits on the pavement of a Temple court and speaks to a ring of seated listeners, while robed elders stand watching at the back.
art.significance: Illustrates John 8:20: "These words he spoke in the treasury, as he taught in the temple."
art.symbolism: The bright figure of Jesus at the center of the gathering echoes his claim to be the light of the world.
art.impact: Places the saying in a real setting: the busy Court of the Women, where the offering chests stood.

events.title: "Before Abraham was, I am"
people: The Jews who had believed in him
events.summary: Jesus warns that those who do not believe will die in their sins, and promises that the truth will make his followers free. His hearers claim Abraham as their father, and the argument grows sharp. When Jesus says, "Before Abraham was, I am," they pick up stones to throw at him. He hides himself and goes out of the Temple.

scripture.text: Jesus then said to the Jews who had believed in him, "If you continue in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free."
Jesus said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am."

echoes.note: God's name revealed to Moses: "I AM WHO I AM."

art.title: The Jews Took Up Rocks to Stone Jesus
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Among the timber scaffolding of the unfinished Temple buildings, an angry crowd bends to snatch up stones, while Jesus walks calmly away out of the scene.
art.significance: Illustrates the end of John 8, when Jesus "hid himself, and went out of the temple."
art.symbolism: The building works recall that Herod's Temple was still being finished in Jesus' day (John 2:20); the loose stones become weapons.
art.impact: A vivid reminder of how close Jesus came to death in Jerusalem months before the Passion.

art.title: He Who is of God Hears the Word of God
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Jesus stands in a colonnade, one hand raised, speaking to a group seated along a low wall; some listen, others turn away.
art.significance: Illustrates John 8:47: "He who is of God hears the words of God."
art.symbolism: The divided audience mirrors the division John describes: some believe, others reject him.
art.impact: One of the many quiet teaching scenes in Tissot's cycle that slow the reader down to listen.

events.title: The man born blind
events.summary: The disciples ask whose sin caused a man to be born blind. Jesus says neither his nor his parents'; it is so that God's works may be shown. He makes clay with spittle, anoints the man's eyes and sends him to wash in the Pool of Siloam, and he comes back seeing. Because it is a sabbath, the Pharisees question him and his parents and finally cast him out. Jesus finds him, and the man believes and worships him.
events.journey: Under a mile, from the Temple down to the pool at the south end of the City of David.

scripture.text: As he said this, he spat on the ground and made clay of the spittle and anointed the man's eyes with the clay, saying to him, "Go, wash in the pool of Siloam" (which means Sent). So he went and washed and came back seeing.
