He answered, "Whether he is a sinner, I do not know; one thing I know, that though I was blind, now I see."

echoes.note: "Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened."
"The waters of Shiloah that go softly", the same spring-fed water system.

art.title: Healing of the Man Born Blind
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.description: Christ, in red and blue, touches the eyes of the kneeling blind man, while disciples and onlookers react around them in a broad piazza of classical buildings.
art.significance: Painted in Italy by the young El Greco, who treated this subject in several versions; the Venetian colors and deep perspective show what he learned from Titian and Tintoretto.
art.symbolism: The long, empty street behind the figures leads the eye into the distance, as sight is given; the arguing groups recall the debate that follows the miracle.
art.impact: A key work for understanding El Greco before his move to Spain.

art.title: The Blind Man Washes in the Pool of Siloam
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Under a great stone arch, a man kneels at the edge of a pool and splashes water on his face, while people draw water nearby.
art.significance: Tissot sketched the pool as it looked in the 1880s, long before the Second Temple pool was found in 2004.
art.symbolism: The water of Siloam, which John translates as "Sent", points to Jesus, the one sent by the Father.
art.impact: Shows the obedient act that brings the healing: "So he went and washed and came back seeing."

events.orderNote: John does not say where Jesus met the man, only that he washed in Siloam. A stepped pool of the Second Temple period was uncovered in 2004 a little south of the older Byzantine pool, and is widely identified as the Pool of Siloam of Jesus' day.

events.title: The Good Shepherd
events.summary: Still speaking to the Pharisees after the healing of the blind man, Jesus contrasts the shepherd who enters by the door with thieves and hirelings. He is the door of the sheep and the good shepherd who knows his own. He will lay down his life for the sheep, and take it up again, by his own will. Once more his hearers are divided.
events.journey: Under a mile, back up to the Temple area.

scripture.text: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
I am the good shepherd; I know my own and my own know me, as the Father knows me and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for the sheep.

echoes.note: God promises to search for his scattered sheep and shepherd them himself.
"The Lord is my shepherd."

art.title: The Parable of the Good Shepherd
art.artist: Philip Galle after Pieter Bruegel the Elder
art.medium: Engraving
art.description: Christ stands in the doorway of a sheepfold carrying a lamb on his shoulders, sheep at his feet. All around, thieves break through the roof and walls and wolves attack the flock.
art.significance: A print published after a design by Bruegel. The Latin over the door reads "Ego sum ostium ovium", "I am the door of the sheep" (John 10:7).
art.symbolism: The shepherd who enters by the door is set against those who climb in "by another way"; the image is often read as a comment on the religious conflicts of Bruegel's day.
art.impact: Spread widely as a print, it is one of the fullest pictures of John 10 ever made.
art.credit: Musea Brugge, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

events.orderNote: John gives no place; Robertson simply says Jerusalem. Some scholars join John 9–10:21 to the Feast of Dedication, but Robertson thinks John 10:24 implies a gap of time.

events.title: The mission of the Seventy
events.summary: Jesus sends out seventy others two by two into every town where he himself is about to come. They are to travel light, bring peace to each house, heal the sick and announce that the kingdom of God has come near. They return full of joy that even the demons submit to them. Jesus rejoices in the Holy Spirit and thanks the Father for revealing these things to little ones.
events.journey: Luke names no towns. Robertson places this ministry in the Judean countryside, a few miles out from Jerusalem.

scripture.text: And he said to them, "The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; pray therefore the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.
The seventy returned with joy, saying, "Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!" And he said to them, "I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.

echoes.note: Moses chooses seventy elders to share his spirit and his work.

art.title: He Sent Them Out Two by Two
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Pairs of disciples with staffs set off in different directions across rolling hills, while Jesus stands among them, sending them on their way.
art.significance: Tissot's title comes from Mark's sending of the Twelve, but Luke uses the same words for the Seventy: "two by two, into every town and place."
art.symbolism: Going in pairs gave each witness a companion, as the Law required two witnesses.
art.impact: Shows how far and wide the mission spread over the countryside.

events.orderNote: Manuscripts differ between seventy and seventy-two (the RSV-2CE reads seventy). Robertson places Luke 10–13:21 in Judea between Tabernacles and Dedication, while many scholars read it as part of the long journey to Jerusalem that begins in Luke 9:51.

events.title: The Good Samaritan
events.summary: A lawyer asks what he must do to inherit eternal life, and answers his own question: love God, and love your neighbor as yourself. "And who is my neighbor?" Jesus tells of a man beaten by robbers on the road down from Jerusalem to Jericho. A priest and a Levite pass by, but a Samaritan, a despised outsider, binds his wounds and pays for his care. "Go and do likewise."

scripture.text: And he answered, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and with all your mind; and your neighbor as yourself."

But a Samaritan, as he journeyed, came to where he was; and when he saw him, he had compassion, and went to him and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine; then he set him on his own beast and brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
Which of these three, do you think, proved neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?" He said, "The one who showed mercy on him." And Jesus said to him, "Go and do likewise."

echoes.note: The Shema: love the Lord your God with all your heart.
"You shall love your neighbor as yourself."

art.title: The Good Samaritan (after Delacroix)
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.description: In swirling yellows and blues, the Samaritan heaves the wounded man onto his horse, while the priest and the Levite walk away along the road in the distance.
art.significance: Painted in May 1890 at the asylum in Saint-Rémy, from a print of Eugène Delacroix's painting of the scene. Van Gogh often made such "translations" into color.
art.symbolism: The straining body of the Samaritan shows love as hard physical work; the empty box at his feet hints at the robbery.
art.impact: One of the best known religious images of modern art, painted only two months before Van Gogh's death.

art.title: The Good Samaritan
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: In a rocky, barren gully, the Samaritan crouches to lift the injured man, his saddled animals waiting on the bank above.
art.significance: Tissot set the scene in the real desert landscape of the road from Jerusalem down to Jericho, which he had traveled.
art.symbolism: The empty hills stress how alone the victim was, and how freely the stranger chose to stop.
art.impact: Helps the reader see why the road was so dangerous.

events.orderNote: The parable is set on the steep, lonely road from Jerusalem down to Jericho, which falls about 3,300 feet in some 17 miles. The "Inn of the Good Samaritan" on that road is a later tradition; Luke does not say where the parable itself was told.

events.title: Martha and Mary
events.summary: Jesus is welcomed into the home of Martha. Her sister Mary sits at his feet and listens, while Martha is busy with much serving and asks Jesus to tell Mary to help. Jesus answers gently that Martha is anxious about many things, but one thing is needful. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken from her.
events.stay: A guest in Martha's house. Robertson notes that Bethany became his Jerusalem home in Passion Week.
events.journey: A few miles across the Judean hills.

scripture.text: But the Lord answered her, "Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things; one thing is needful. Mary has chosen the good portion, which shall not be taken away from her."

art.title: Christ in the House of Martha and Mary
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.description: Christ sits at a table, turning to Mary, who rests her head on her hand at his feet, while Martha leans in with a basket of bread.
art.significance: One of Vermeer's earliest known works and his largest painting, made before he turned to the quiet interiors for which he is famous.
art.symbolism: Christ's gesture links the two sisters: his hand points to Mary, but his face turns toward Martha, holding both service and listening together.
art.impact: Rediscovered in 1901; its signature helped scholars trace Vermeer's early career.

art.title: Kitchen Scene with Christ in the House of Martha and Mary
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.description: In a Spanish kitchen, a sulking young cook pounds garlic beside fish and eggs while an old woman points her toward a small scene of Christ with Martha and Mary in the background.
art.significance: Painted by Velázquez at about nineteen in Seville. It is a bodegón, a kitchen still life, with the Gospel story seen through an opening.
art.symbolism: The young cook is a Martha of Seville, busy with "much serving"; the old woman seems to remind her of the "one thing needful."
art.impact: A celebrated early masterpiece, and a striking example of a Gospel scene placed inside everyday life.

events.orderNote: Luke says only "a village". John 11:1 names Bethany as the village of Mary and Martha, so Robertson places the visit there, near Jerusalem, and not at Bethany beyond the Jordan.

events.title: "Lord, teach us to pray"
events.summary: After Jesus has been praying, a disciple asks him to teach them to pray, as John taught his disciples. Jesus gives them a short form of the Lord's Prayer. He adds the parable of a friend who knocks at midnight to borrow bread and is answered because he persists. "Ask, and it will be given you"; how much more will the Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him.
events.journey: About 1 to 2 miles, from Bethany up over the Mount of Olives.

scripture.text: And he said to them, "When you pray, say: "Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. Give us each day our daily bread; and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive every one who is indebted to us; and lead us not into temptation."
And I tell you, Ask, and it will be given you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.

art.title: Jerusalem Seen from the Mount of Olives
art.medium: Drawing on paper
art.description: A panoramic study of the walled city across the Kidron Valley, drawn from the slope of the Mount of Olives with olive trees and terraces in the foreground.
art.significance: One of the landscape studies Tissot made in Palestine as material for his Life of Christ.
art.symbolism: The view takes in the city Jesus prayed over and taught near; the Mount of Olives was a place he often went to pray (Luke 22:39).
art.impact: Shows the setting tradition gives to the teaching of the Lord's Prayer, just above the Garden of Gethsemane.

events.orderNote: Luke says only "in a certain place." Robertson suggests Judea. Since the Middle Ages, tradition has placed the teaching of the Lord's Prayer at a cave on the Mount of Olives, under the ruins of Constantine's 4th-century Eleona church; the Pater Noster church stands there today. Matthew gives a longer form in the Sermon on the Mount; Robertson takes this as a second teaching.

events.title: By the finger of God
people: A man who had been mute
events.summary: Jesus casts out a demon that had made a man mute. Some say he does it by Beelzebul, the prince of demons. He answers that a divided kingdom cannot stand, and that if he casts out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come. A woman calls out a blessing on his mother; he answers, "Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!" He warns that this generation will get no sign but the sign of Jonah.
events.journey: A few miles back into the Judean countryside.

scripture.text: But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.

As he said this, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him, "Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked!" But he said, "Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!"

echoes.note: Pharaoh's magicians: "This is the finger of God."
The people of Nineveh repent at Jonah's preaching.

art.title: A Woman Cries Out in a Crowd
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: In a crowded street of tall stone houses, a woman lifts her arms and calls out toward Jesus over the heads of the throng.
art.significance: Illustrates Luke 11:27, a moment found only in Luke.
art.symbolism: The woman praises Mary's motherhood; Jesus answers that hearing and keeping God's word is the greater blessing, which Mary herself did.
art.impact: Catches the noisy, spontaneous mood of Jesus' teaching among ordinary people.

events.orderNote: Matthew and Mark tell a similar charge of league with Beelzebul in Galilee (§61). Robertson thinks it natural that the accusation was repeated a year or so later in Judea; others take Luke's account as the same event placed by theme.

events.title: Woes at a Pharisee's table
events.summary: A Pharisee invites Jesus to a meal and is astonished that he does not first wash. Jesus says they clean the outside of the cup while inside they are full of greed. He pronounces woes on Pharisees who tithe herbs but neglect justice and the love of God, and on lawyers who load others with burdens. From then on the scribes and Pharisees press him hard, lying in wait to catch him in something he might say.
events.stay: A guest at a Pharisee's midday meal.

scripture.text: "But woe to you Pharisees! for you tithe mint and rue and every herb, and neglect justice and the love of God; these you ought to have done, without neglecting the others.

echoes.note: "To do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God."

art.title: Curses Against the Pharisees
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Jesus rises at a banquet table under a colonnade and stretches out his arm in rebuke, while the reclining guests recoil and argue.
art.significance: Tissot sets the woes at a meal, as Luke does in chapter 11.
art.symbolism: The laden table and the angry faces set outward piety against inward greed, the theme of Jesus' words about cup and dish.
art.impact: A dramatic picture of the growing break between Jesus and the Pharisees.

events.title: The rich fool, and do not be anxious
events.summary: With thousands crowding around, Jesus warns his disciples against the leaven of the Pharisees and tells them not to fear. When a man asks him to settle an inheritance, he tells of a rich fool who builds bigger barns and dies that very night. He tells them not to be anxious, like the ravens and the lilies, and to be like servants waiting for their master's return. He speaks of the baptism he must undergo, and of the division his coming will bring.

scripture.text: But God said to him, 'Fool! This night your soul is required of you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?' So is he who lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God."
Consider the lilies, how they grow; they neither toil nor spin; yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these.
"Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom.

echoes.note: A man grows rich and says, "I have found rest", not knowing his time will pass.
When the rich man dies he will carry nothing away.

art.title: The Parable of the Rich Fool
art.medium: Oil on oak panel
art.description: An old man in a cluttered room full of ledgers, money bags and papers holds a coin up to a candle and peers at it through his spectacles.
art.significance: An early work painted in Leiden when Rembrandt was about 21. It is also known as "The Money Changer."
art.symbolism: The candle, hidden by his hand, lights only the coin and his face: the man's whole world has shrunk to his money, with the dark pressing in around him.
art.impact: One of Rembrandt's first experiments with dramatic candlelight, a hallmark of his later art.

art.title: The Man Who Hoards
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: A rich man sits brooding among bulging sacks of grain, while a shadowy figure with a blade looms in the gloom above him.
art.significance: Illustrates the parable of Luke 12:16–21.
art.symbolism: The hidden figure behind him stands for the death he has not planned for: "This night your soul is required of you."
art.impact: Turns the parable into a chilling image that is easy to remember.

events.orderNote: Much of this teaching also appears in Matthew's Sermon on the Mount and other discourses. Robertson notes that Jesus often repeated his favorite sayings on different occasions.

events.title: Repent or perish: the barren fig tree
people: Some who told him of the Galileans
events.summary: Some tell Jesus of Galileans whose blood Pilate mingled with their sacrifices. He asks whether they, or the eighteen killed when the tower in Siloam fell, were worse sinners than others, and answers: "Unless you repent you will all likewise perish." Then he tells of a fig tree that has borne no fruit for three years. The vinedresser begs for one more year to dig around it and manure it.

scripture.text: I tell you, No; but unless you repent you will all likewise perish.
And he answered him, 'Let it alone, sir, this year also, till I dig about it and put on manure. And if it bears fruit next year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.'"

echoes.note: The song of the vineyard that yields wild grapes.

art.title: The Vine Dresser and the Fig Tree
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: A vinedresser crouches with his spade at the roots of a gnarled, leafless fig tree, while the owner stands beside him looking at it.
art.significance: Illustrates the parable of Luke 13:6–9.
art.symbolism: The bare tree stands for a people given time to bear fruit; the digging and manure are the patient mercy that pleads for one more year.
art.impact: Draws attention to the vinedresser, whose plea many readers see as an image of Christ interceding.

art.title: The Tower of Siloam
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: A stone tower collapses in a cloud of dust, its beams and blocks crashing down as people run for their lives from the archway below.
art.significance: Illustrates Luke 13:4, the disaster Jesus mentions, known only from this verse.
art.symbolism: The sudden fall makes Jesus' point: death can come to anyone without warning, so repent now.
art.impact: Turns a passing remark into a vivid scene.

events.orderNote: Neither tragedy is recorded outside Luke. Pilate's harshness is known from Josephus, and the tower of Siloam probably stood on the walls near the pool.

events.title: The bent woman healed on the sabbath
people: A woman bent over for eighteen years
events.summary: Teaching in a synagogue on the sabbath, Jesus sees a woman who has been bent double for eighteen years. He lays his hands on her and she stands up straight and praises God. The ruler of the synagogue protests; Jesus answers that they untie an ox or donkey on the sabbath, so surely this daughter of Abraham should be set free. He repeats the parables of the mustard seed and the leaven.

scripture.text: And when Jesus saw her, he called her and said to her, "Woman, you are freed from your infirmity." And he laid his hands upon her, and immediately she was made straight, and she praised God.
And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan bound for eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the sabbath day?"

echoes.note: The sabbath as a remembrance of Israel's release from bondage.

art.title: The Woman with an Infirmity of Eighteen Years
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: In a synagogue hung with lamps, a woman bent almost double stands before Jesus as he reaches toward her; the elders on the benches look on.
art.significance: Illustrates Luke 13:10–17, a healing found only in Luke.
art.symbolism: Her bent body pictures bondage; Jesus calls her "a daughter of Abraham" and sets her free on the day of rest.
art.impact: Shows the public, sabbath setting that sparked the ruler's protest.

events.title: At the Feast of Dedication
events.summary: It is winter, the feast of Hanukkah, and Jesus is walking in Solomon's portico in the Temple. The Jews gather round and demand that he tell them plainly whether he is the Christ. He points to his works, says his sheep hear his voice, and declares, "I and the Father are one." They take up stones again and try to arrest him, but he escapes from their hands.
events.journey: A few miles back to Jerusalem.

scripture.text: My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, and no one shall snatch them out of my hand.
I and the Father are one."

echoes.note: Judas Maccabeus rededicates the altar in 164 BC and decrees the yearly eight-day feast.
"I say, 'You are gods'", which Jesus quotes in his defense.

art.title: Jesus Walks in the Portico of Solomon
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Jesus, in white, walks with his disciples through a long colonnade of the Temple, while people sit and talk in the shade of the columns.
art.significance: Illustrates John 10:23, set in winter at the Feast of Dedication.
art.symbolism: Solomon's portico on the east side of the Temple recalls the king who built the first Temple, where Jesus now claims to be one with the Father.
art.impact: Later the apostles also gathered in Solomon's portico (Acts 3:11; 5:12).

events.orderNote: Robertson dates this to December AD 29, about two months after Tabernacles and three to four months before the crucifixion.

events.title: Withdrawal beyond the Jordan
people: The people who came to him
events.summary: Jesus leaves Jerusalem and goes back across the Jordan to the place where John had first baptized, and stays there. Many come to him. They say that John did no sign, but everything John said about this man was true. Many believe in him there.
events.stay: He stayed some time at the place where John had baptized, in Perea, under Herod Antipas.
events.journey: About 25 miles, down the desert road to Jericho and across the Jordan, a long day or two on foot.

scripture.text: And many came to him; and they said, "John did no sign, but everything that John said about this man was true." And many believed in him there.

art.title: Al-Maghtas, Bethany beyond the Jordan
art.medium: Photograph
art.description: Excavated pools and stone steps at the baptism site east of the Jordan, under modern shelters, beside the wooded river valley.
art.significance: Al-Maghtas has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2015. Excavations found churches, pools and hermit caves from the Roman and Byzantine periods.
art.symbolism: Jesus returns to the place where John had first pointed him out, and finds that John's witness has borne fruit.
art.impact: Helps the reader picture the quiet refuge across the river, out of reach of the Jerusalem authorities.
art.credit: Photo: Producer, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

events.orderNote: Robertson places Luke 13:22 to 17:10 in this Perean period between Dedication and the raising of Lazarus. Many scholars instead read Luke's material as one long final journey to Jerusalem.

events.title: "Go and tell that fox"
people: Someone who asked about the saved
events.summary: Jesus goes through towns and villages teaching, journeying toward Jerusalem. Asked whether few will be saved, he says to strive to enter by the narrow door. Some Pharisees warn him that Herod Antipas wants to kill him. He sends word to "that fox" that he will finish his work, for a prophet cannot perish away from Jerusalem, and he laments over the city that kills the prophets.
events.journey: Luke says only "through towns and villages"; Perea lay along the east side of the Jordan Valley.

scripture.text: And he said to them, "Go and tell that fox, 'Behold, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and the third day I finish my course.

O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, killing the prophets and stoning those who are sent to you! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you would not!

echoes.note: "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord", quoted at the end of the lament.
"This house shall become a desolation."

art.title: He Went Through the Villages on the Way to Jerusalem
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Jesus and his disciples pass a hillside village of flat-roofed stone houses, as people come out from the houses to see him.
art.significance: Illustrates Luke 13:22: "He went on his way through towns and villages, teaching, and journeying toward Jerusalem."
art.symbolism: The road keeps leading on toward Jerusalem, where Jesus says a prophet must die.
art.impact: Captures the slow, village-by-village movement of this part of the ministry.

events.orderNote: Matthew places a nearly identical lament over Jerusalem in the Temple during Holy Week (Matthew 23:37–39). Robertson treats them as two occasions.

events.title: Dropsy healed, and the great banquet
events.summary: Dining on the sabbath at the house of a leading Pharisee, Jesus heals a man with dropsy and silences his critics. Seeing guests choose the places of honor, he tells them to take the lowest place. He tells his host to invite the poor, the maimed, the lame and the blind. Then he tells of a great banquet whose invited guests all make excuses, so the master fills his house with the poor and with people from the highways and hedges.
events.stay: A guest at a sabbath meal in a Pharisee's house.

scripture.text: For every one who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted."
But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. You will be repaid at the resurrection of the just."
And the master said to the servant, 'Go out to the highways and hedges, and compel people to come in, that my house may be filled.

echoes.note: Do not put yourself forward; better to be told, "Come up here."
The Lord's feast of rich food for all peoples on his mountain.

art.title: The Parable of the Great Banquet
art.medium: Oil on panel
art.description: A crowded Renaissance palace: in the foreground the poor and the crippled are brought in from the street, while the feast goes on at tables in the halls beyond.
art.significance: By an unidentified Antwerp master named after a monogram on a painting in Brunswick. He set Gospel scenes among the busy street life of his own day.
art.symbolism: The people of the highways and hedges fill the master's house, while the invited guests are nowhere to be seen.
art.impact: A rare large painting of this parable, packed with lively details of 16th-century Flemish life.

events.orderNote: Matthew's parable of the wedding feast (Matthew 22:1–14), told in Holy Week, is similar. Robertson treats them as two different parables.

events.title: Count the cost
events.summary: Great crowds are following him. Jesus turns and tells them that anyone who does not bear his own cross and come after him cannot be his disciple. A man who builds a tower first sits down and counts the cost; a king going to war first weighs his strength. So whoever does not renounce all that he has cannot be his disciple. Salt that has lost its taste is thrown away.

scripture.text: Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me, cannot be my disciple.
For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it?

art.title: Jesus Traveling
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Jesus and his disciples walk along a broad hillside track, followed at a distance by other travelers and pack animals.
art.significance: Pictures the scene of Luke 14:25: "Now great multitudes accompanied him; and he turned and said to them..."
art.symbolism: The long road and the following crowd frame Jesus' warning: to follow him all the way means carrying the cross.
art.impact: Helps the reader picture the long walks between the places on this map.

events.title: The lost sheep and the lost coin
events.summary: Tax collectors and sinners come near to hear Jesus, and the Pharisees and scribes grumble that he receives sinners and eats with them. He answers with parables. A shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to find one lost sheep and carries it home rejoicing. A woman lights a lamp and sweeps the house until she finds her lost silver coin. So there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.

scripture.text: "What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness, and go after the one which is lost, until he finds it?
Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents."

echoes.note: "I will seek the lost, and I will bring back the strayed."

art.title: The Lost Drachma
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: In a dark house, a woman crouches on the stone floor beside a small oil lamp, searching every corner for her lost coin.
art.significance: Illustrates the parable of Luke 15:8–10.
art.symbolism: The lamp and the sweeping show God's careful, personal search for each one who is lost.
art.impact: Brings out the homely detail of the parable: a poor woman for whom one silver coin truly matters.

events.orderNote: Matthew gives the lost sheep in a different setting, a lesson to the disciples about little ones (Matthew 18:12–14, §91).

events.title: The prodigal son
events.summary: A younger son takes his share of his father's property and squanders it in a far country. Starving and feeding pigs, he comes to himself and goes home to confess. While he is still far off his father runs to embrace him, clothes him and kills the fatted calf. The elder son refuses to join the feast, and the father pleads with him: his brother was dead and is alive again, was lost and is found.

scripture.text: And he arose and came to his father. But while he was yet at a distance, his father saw him and had compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.
And he said to him, 'Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to make merry and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.'"

echoes.note: Esau runs to meet Jacob, embraces him and kisses him.

art.title: The Return of the Prodigal Son
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.description: The ragged son kneels with his shaven head pressed against his father's chest; the old father, in a red cloak, lays both hands on his back. The elder brother stands to the right, stiff and apart.
art.significance: One of Rembrandt's last works, painted near the end of his life.
art.symbolism: The father's two hands are painted differently, one broad and strong, one gentle, often read as a father's and a mother's love together.
art.impact: Among the most loved religious paintings in the world; Henri Nouwen's book on it (1992) made it famous to millions.

art.title: The Prodigal Son Begging
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: The younger son, thin and in rags, stands alone on a hillside with a shepherd's crook, the pigs he tends rooting behind him.
art.significance: Illustrates Luke 15:15–16, the son's lowest point.
art.symbolism: Feeding pigs, unclean animals to a Jew, shows how far he has fallen before he "came to himself."
art.impact: Makes the son's misery concrete, so the welcome home feels all the greater.

events.title: The dishonest steward
events.summary: A rich man's steward is about to be dismissed for wasting his goods. He quickly calls in his master's debtors and reduces their bills, so that they will welcome him later. The master commends him for his shrewdness. Jesus tells his disciples to use worldly wealth to make friends for eternity, for no one can serve two masters. The Pharisees, lovers of money, scoff at him.

scripture.text: "He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much; and he who is dishonest in a very little is dishonest also in much.
No servant can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and mammon."

art.title: The Parable of the Unjust Steward
art.medium: Oil on panel
art.description: A rich master in a fur-trimmed coat sits at a desk crowded with ledgers and papers, raising his hand as his steward, in red, looks up anxiously.
art.significance: Marinus van Reymerswaele and his followers specialized in sharp-eyed scenes of bankers, tax collectors and stewards at their accounts.
art.symbolism: The account books stand for the reckoning: "Turn in the account of your stewardship."
art.impact: Shows how Netherlandish painters used the parable to comment on money and business in their own day.

events.title: The rich man and Lazarus
events.summary: A rich man feasts every day in purple and fine linen, while a poor man named Lazarus lies at his gate covered with sores. Both die. Lazarus is carried by angels to Abraham's bosom; the rich man is in torment in Hades. Abraham tells him a great chasm is fixed between them, and that if his brothers do not hear Moses and the prophets, they will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead.

scripture.text: But Abraham said, 'Son, remember that you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner evil things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish.
He said to him, 'If they do not hear Moses and the prophets, neither will they be convinced if some one should rise from the dead.'"

echoes.note: Woe to those who lie on beds of ivory and feast, but do not grieve over the ruin of Joseph.

art.title: The Poor Lazarus at the Rich Man's Door
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Lazarus, wrapped in rags, sits on the cobbles by the steps of a great stone house while stray dogs lick his sores.
art.significance: Illustrates Luke 16:20–21.
art.symbolism: The closed door and the dogs set the rich man's indifference against the poor man's need; only the dogs show him any care.
art.impact: Tissot also painted the sequel, the rich man in torment.

events.orderNote: This is the only parable in which a character is given a name. Medieval tradition called the rich man "Dives", Latin for "rich".

events.title: Faith, forgiveness and unworthy servants
events.summary: Jesus warns his disciples not to cause little ones to sin, and tells them to forgive a brother who repents, even seven times a day. The apostles say, "Increase our faith!" He answers that faith as small as a grain of mustard seed could uproot a tree. A servant who has done all he was told has only done his duty, and should say, "We are unworthy servants."

scripture.text: And the Lord said, "If you had faith as a grain of mustard seed, you could say to this sycamine tree, 'Be rooted up, and be planted in the sea,' and it would obey you.
So you also, when you have done all that is commanded you, say, 'We are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty.'"

art.title: The Man at the Plough
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: A farmer drives a plough pulled by a pair of donkeys across a stony hillside field.
art.significance: A scene of everyday farm work, the kind of labor Jesus uses in Luke 17:7: "Will any one of you, who has a servant plowing..."
art.symbolism: The servant who has plowed all day still serves his master's supper: duty done is not a claim on reward.
art.impact: Shows the hard, ordinary work behind Jesus' images of service.

events.title: The raising of Lazarus
events.summary: Martha and Mary send word that their brother Lazarus is ill. Jesus waits two days, then goes back to Judea, though the disciples fear he will be stoned. Lazarus has been in the tomb four days. Jesus tells Martha, "I am the resurrection and the life", and she confesses him as the Christ. Jesus weeps, has the stone taken away, and cries, "Lazarus, come out." The dead man walks out, still bound in his grave clothes.
events.stay: He stayed outside the village at first; Martha and then Mary came out to meet him.
events.journey: Probably 25 to 30 miles from Perea, across the Jordan, through Jericho and up the desert road, a journey of a day or two.

scripture.text: Jesus said to her, "I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and whoever lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?"
Jesus wept.

When he had said this, he cried with a loud voice, "Lazarus, come out." The dead man came out, his hands and feet bound with bandages, and his face wrapped with a cloth. Jesus said to them, "Unbind him, and let him go."

echoes.note: "I will open your graves, and raise you from your graves, O my people."

art.title: The Raising of Lazarus
art.medium: Fresco
art.description: Christ raises his hand toward Lazarus, who stands in the mouth of the tomb wrapped like a mummy. Martha and Mary kneel at Jesus' feet, and onlookers cover their noses.
art.significance: Part of Giotto's cycle of the lives of the Virgin and Christ, a turning point in Western painting.
art.symbolism: The grave clothes, still grey with death, face the living gesture of Christ; it foreshadows Christ's own resurrection, shown in the same chapel.
art.impact: Giotto's solid, human figures and real emotion opened the way to the Renaissance.

art.title: The Raising of Lazarus
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.description: In a dark, bare room, men lift the stiff body of Lazarus from the tomb as Christ, at the left, points toward him. A beam of light falls across Lazarus, whose arms open in the shape of a cross.
art.significance: Painted in Sicily while Caravaggio was on the run, for a merchant family named Lazzari.
art.symbolism: Lazarus is caught between death and life: one hand falls toward a skull, the other opens toward the light.
art.impact: One of the great works of Caravaggio's last years.

events.orderNote: Robertson notes that Jesus seems to have been two or three days' journey away (John 11:6, 17), probably in Perea. A tomb cut in the rock at al-Eizariya (the town's Arabic name comes from "Lazarus") has been honored as Lazarus's tomb since at least the 4th century.

events.title: Caiaphas's counsel; retreat to Ephraim
events.summary: Many who saw Lazarus raised believe in Jesus, but some report it to the Pharisees. The council meets, afraid that the Romans will come and destroy the Temple and the nation. Caiaphas, high priest that year, says it is better that one man should die for the people; John sees in this an unwitting prophecy. From that day they plan to put him to death, so Jesus withdraws with his disciples to a town called Ephraim, near the wilderness.
events.stay: He stayed at Ephraim with his disciples until shortly before the Passover.
events.journey: About 14 miles north from Bethany into the hills near the wilderness.

scripture.text: But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, "You know nothing at all; you do not understand that it is expedient for you that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish."
Jesus therefore no longer went about openly among the Jews, but went from there to the country near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim; and there he stayed with the disciples.

art.title: He Went on His Way to Ephraim
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Jesus and a few disciples walk down a rocky path among olive trees and steep banks, away from Jerusalem.
art.significance: Illustrates John 11:54.
art.symbolism: The narrow, lonely path pictures his withdrawal after the council's decision to put him to death.
art.impact: A rare image of this little-known retreat before the last Passover.

events.orderNote: Ephraim is usually identified with et-Taiyiba (Taybeh), about 4 miles northeast of Bethel, the Ophrah of the Old Testament. Robertson thinks it lay in the north of Judea.

events.title: The ten lepers
events.summary: On the way to Jerusalem, passing between Samaria and Galilee, Jesus is met by ten lepers who stand far off and cry for mercy. He sends them to show themselves to the priests, and on the way they are made clean. Only one, a Samaritan, comes back praising God and falls at Jesus' feet. Asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God will come, Jesus says it is "in the midst of you", and warns the disciples of the sudden day of the Son of man.
events.journey: About 40 miles north from Ephraim along the hill road through Samaria, past Sychar, to the edge of the Jezreel Valley.

scripture.text: Then one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice; and he fell on his face at Jesus' feet, giving him thanks. Now he was a Samaritan.

Being asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God was coming, he answered them, "The kingdom of God is not coming with signs to be observed; nor will they say, 'Lo, here it is!' or 'There!' for behold, the kingdom of God is in the midst of you."

echoes.note: The leper must live apart and cry, "Unclean, unclean."
Naaman the Syrian, a foreigner, is cleansed and returns to give thanks.

art.title: The Healing of Ten Lepers
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: On a rocky hillside outside a town, ten lepers wrapped in cloths kneel and raise their arms toward Jesus, who stands at a distance in white.
art.significance: Illustrates Luke 17:11–19.
art.symbolism: The lepers keep their distance as the Law required; the healing that follows lets them return to their families.
art.impact: Shows the scene from far off, as Luke says they "stood at a distance."

events.orderNote: Robertson follows Wieseler: from Ephraim Jesus went north through Samaria to the edge of Galilee, to join the Galilean pilgrims going down through Perea. That explains why Luke names Samaria first. The village is not named; a tradition places it at Burqin near Jenin.

events.title: The widow and the judge; the Pharisee and the tax collector
events.summary: To teach that they ought always to pray and not lose heart, Jesus tells of a widow who keeps coming to an unjust judge until he gives her justice. How much more will God vindicate his elect who cry to him day and night. Then he tells of a Pharisee who thanks God he is not like other men, and a tax collector who stands far off and beats his breast. It is the tax collector who goes home justified.

scripture.text: And will not God vindicate his elect, who cry to him day and night? Will he delay long over them?

But the tax collector, standing far off, would not even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, 'God, be merciful to me a sinner!' I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for every one who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted."

echoes.note: "The prayer of the humble pierces the clouds."

art.title: The Pharisee and the Publican
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: In a richly decorated Temple hall, a Pharisee in a prayer shawl stands upright in the foreground, while the tax collector hides by a pillar in the back, head bowed.
art.significance: Illustrates Luke 18:10–14.
art.symbolism: Distance and posture tell the story: the proud man stands forward, the humble one stays far off and will not lift his eyes.
art.impact: A clear picture of the reversal at the heart of the parable.

events.orderNote: Luke gives no place for these parables. Robertson places them on the last journey, after the healing of the ten lepers and before Jesus crosses into Perea.

events.title: On marriage and divorce
events.summary: Jesus leaves Galilee and comes into the region of Judea beyond the Jordan, and crowds gather again. Pharisees test him: is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife? He points back to creation: God made them male and female, and the two become one flesh. What God has joined together, no one must separate; Moses allowed divorce because of their hardness of heart. In the house the disciples ask again, and he speaks of those who renounce marriage for the kingdom.
events.journey: About 45 miles, east through the Jezreel Valley to Scythopolis, across the Jordan and south through Perea with the Galilean pilgrims.

scripture.text: What therefore God has joined together, let not man put asunder."

echoes.note: "A man leaves his father and his mother and cleaves to his wife, and they become one flesh."
The certificate of divorce the Pharisees cite.

art.title: The Scribe Stood to Tempt Jesus
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: On a stony hillside, a man in a striped robe stands and questions Jesus, who sits among his disciples; the Judean hills stretch away behind.
art.significance: Tissot made it for the lawyer's test in Luke 10:25. It fits this scene too, where the Pharisees come "to test him" with a question of the Law.
art.symbolism: The standing questioner and the seated teacher set a challenge against calm authority.
art.impact: Shows the open-air setting in which such debates took place along the road.

events.orderNote: Here Matthew and Mark rejoin the story after a long gap. Matthew 19:1 links this departure to the end of the Galilean teaching (§92), and Robertson notes that we must suppose a break in their narrative. Matthew alone includes the exception "except for unchastity".

Mt.text: And I say to you: whoever divorces his wife, except for unchastity, and marries another, commits adultery; and he who marries a divorced woman, commits adultery."

Mk.text: And he said to them, "Whoever divorces his wife and marries another, commits adultery against her; and if she divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery."

events.title: Let the children come to me
events.summary: People bring little children, even infants, to Jesus so that he might touch them and pray for them. The disciples rebuke them. Jesus is indignant: the kingdom of God belongs to such as these, and whoever does not receive it like a child shall not enter it. He takes the children in his arms and blesses them.

scripture.text: But when Jesus saw it he was indignant, and said to them, "Let the children come to me, do not hinder them; for to such belongs the kingdom of God. Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it."
And he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands upon them.

art.title: Christ Blessing the Children
art.medium: Oil on panel
art.description: Christ holds a baby and lays his hand on others as mothers press around him with their infants; the apostles look on from the left. A German inscription runs across the top.
art.significance: Cranach's workshop painted many versions of this subject, which became popular in Lutheran Germany.
art.symbolism: The infants in their mothers' arms were read as an argument for infant baptism, against the Anabaptists of the day.
art.impact: One of the most recognizable images of the Reformation era.

Mt.text: Then children were brought to him that he might lay his hands on them and pray. The disciples rebuked the people;

Mk.text: And he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands upon them.

Lk.text: Now they were bringing even infants to him that he might touch them; and when the disciples saw it, they rebuked them.

events.title: The rich young ruler
events.summary: A man runs up and kneels, asking what he must do to inherit eternal life. He has kept the commandments from his youth. Jesus looks at him, loves him, and tells him to sell what he has, give to the poor, and follow him; the man goes away sorrowful, for he has great possessions. Jesus says it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom, but with God all things are possible. Those who have left everything will receive a hundredfold and eternal life.

scripture.text: And Jesus looking upon him loved him, and said to him, "You lack one thing; go, sell what you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me."
It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God."
Jesus looked at them and said, "With men it is impossible, but not with God; for all things are possible with God."

echoes.note: The commandments Jesus lists to the young man.

art.title: The Rich Young Man Went Away Sorrowful
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: A young man in fine clothes walks away down a hillside path, head lowered, while Jesus and the disciples stand behind him on the road.
art.significance: Illustrates Mark 10:22.
art.symbolism: He walks toward the viewer and away from Jesus, turning his back on the invitation "come, follow me."
art.impact: Captures the sadness of a calling refused.

events.orderNote: Only Matthew calls him young and only Luke calls him a ruler; Mark alone says that Jesus looked at him and loved him.

Mt.text: The young man said to him, "All these I have observed; what do I still lack?"

Mk.text: And Jesus looking upon him loved him, and said to him, "You lack one thing; go, sell what you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me."

Lk.text: And a ruler asked him, "Good Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?"

events.title: The laborers in the vineyard
events.summary: A householder hires laborers for his vineyard at dawn for a denarius, and goes out again at nine, noon, three and five o'clock to hire more. At evening he pays everyone the same, starting with the last. Those who worked all day grumble. The master answers that he has done them no wrong: may he not be generous with what is his? So the last will be first, and the first last.

scripture.text: Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Or do you begrudge my generosity?' So the last will be first, and the first last."

echoes.note: Pay the hired laborer his wages on the same day, before the sun goes down.

art.title: The Parable of the Laborers in the Vineyard
art.medium: Oil on panel
art.description: In a dim room lit by a tall window, the householder sits at a table as workers crowd in; some take their pay, while one at the front argues.
art.significance: A small, dark panel from Rembrandt's Amsterdam years.
art.symbolism: The light from the window falls on the paying of wages: every worker receives the same denarius, a picture of grace.
art.impact: One of the few paintings of this parable by a major master.

art.title: The First Shall Be Last
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Jesus stands among palm trees and speaks to disciples seated on a low wall around him.
art.significance: Illustrates the saying that frames the parable (Matthew 19:30; 20:16).
art.symbolism: Jesus stands while his hearers sit: the teacher who will take the last place of a servant.
art.impact: Shows the parable as part of Jesus' teaching to his own disciples.

events.title: Going up to Jerusalem: the third passion prediction
events.summary: On the road going up to Jerusalem, Jesus walks ahead and the disciples are amazed and afraid. He takes the Twelve aside and tells them a third time that the Son of man will be condemned, mocked, scourged and killed, and will rise after three days. James and John, with their mother, ask for the seats at his right and left in his glory. Jesus tells the indignant Twelve that whoever would be great must be their servant, for the Son of man came to give his life as a ransom for many.

scripture.text: "Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem; and the Son of man will be delivered to the chief priests and the scribes, and they will condemn him to death, and deliver him to the Gentiles; and they will mock him, and spit upon him, and scourge him, and kill him; and after three days he will rise."
For the Son of man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many."

echoes.note: The Servant who bears the sin of many.

art.title: Christ and the Wife and Sons of Zebedee
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.description: The mother of James and John kneels before Christ, presenting her two sons, while the other apostles look on beside a classical portico.
art.significance: Veronese often set Gospel scenes among the grand architecture and rich fabrics of Venice.
art.symbolism: The kneeling mother asks for glory; Christ will answer by speaking of the cup he must drink.
art.impact: A rare large painting of this request, which Matthew alone puts in the mother's mouth.

events.orderNote: In Mark, James and John make the request themselves; in Matthew their mother asks for them. Robertson places this in Perea, before the crossing of the Jordan to Jericho.

Mt.text: Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came up to him, with her sons, and kneeling before him she asked him for something. And he said to her, "What do you want?" She said to him, "Command that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom."

Mk.text: And they were on the road, going up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was walking ahead of them; and they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid.

Lk.text: And taking the twelve, he said to them, "Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that is written of the Son of man by the prophets will be accomplished.

events.title: Blind Bartimaeus
events.summary: At Jericho a blind beggar, Bartimaeus, hears that Jesus of Nazareth is passing and cries out, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!" The crowd tells him to be quiet, but he cries all the more. Jesus calls him; he throws off his cloak and comes. "Go your way; your faith has made you well", and at once he sees and follows Jesus on the road.
events.journey: About 20 miles, down the Perean side of the valley and across the Jordan ford to Jericho.

scripture.text: And when he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out and say, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!"

And Jesus said to him, "What do you want me to do for you?" And the blind man said to him, "Master, let me receive my sight." And Jesus said to him, "Go your way; your faith has made you well." And immediately he received his sight and followed him on the way.

echoes.note: The blind and the lame among those God gathers home.

art.title: Christ Healing the Blind of Jericho
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.description: Christ reaches out to touch the eyes of a kneeling blind man, while a second blind man gropes forward and the apostles and townspeople watch; a walled town rises behind.
art.significance: Follows Matthew's account of two blind men. It became a model for French academic painters.
art.symbolism: The calm, ordered composition centers on Christ's single touch; the reaching hands of the blind show their faith.
art.impact: In 1667 it was the subject of a famous lecture at the French Royal Academy, used to teach how a picture should tell a story.

art.title: The Two Blind Men at Jericho
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Two blind men stand on a rocky bank by the road, arms raised, calling out, while a crowd streams past below the town walls.
art.significance: Illustrates Matthew 20:29–34.
art.symbolism: Their raised arms and loud cries show the persistence the crowd tries to silence.
art.impact: Puts the reader at the roadside where Bartimaeus sat.

events.orderNote: Matthew has two blind men; Mark and Luke describe one, probably the better known. Mark and Matthew say Jesus was leaving Jericho, Luke that he was drawing near. Robertson suggests he had left the old town and was approaching Herod's new Jericho nearby.

Mt.text: And behold, two blind men sitting by the roadside, when they heard that Jesus was passing by, cried out, "Have mercy on us, Son of David!"

Mk.text: And throwing off his mantle he sprang up and came to Jesus.

Lk.text: And immediately he received his sight and followed him, glorifying God; and all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.

events.date: Spring AD 33, about a week before Passover
events.title: Zacchaeus
events.summary: Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector and rich, wants to see who Jesus is, but he is small, so he climbs a sycamore tree. Jesus stops, calls him by name and says he must stay at his house today. The crowd grumbles that he is the guest of a sinner. Zacchaeus promises half his goods to the poor and fourfold repayment to anyone he has cheated. "Today salvation has come to this house."
events.stay: He stayed as a guest in Zacchaeus' house in Jericho.

scripture.text: And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up and said to him, "Zacchaeus, make haste and come down; for I must stay at your house today."
And Jesus said to him, "Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of man came to seek and to save the lost."

echoes.note: The Law's fourfold restitution for a stolen sheep.

art.title: Zacchaeus in the Sycamore Awaiting the Passage of Jesus
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Zacchaeus, in a yellow robe, straddles a great branch of a sycamore tree; boys climb in the branches, and Jesus and his disciples approach along the road below.
art.significance: Illustrates Luke 19:1–6.
art.symbolism: The rich tax collector, climbing like a child, gives up his dignity to see Jesus.
art.impact: One of the best known images of the story, often reproduced in children's Bibles.

events.orderNote: Jericho's "Zacchaeus tree", an old sycamore fig in the town, is a local tradition.

events.date: Spring AD 33, about a week before Passover
events.title: The parable of the pounds
events.summary: Because he is near Jerusalem and the people think the kingdom will appear at once, Jesus tells a parable. A nobleman goes to a far country to receive a kingdom, leaving ten servants a pound each to trade with, while his citizens send word that they do not want him to reign. On his return he rewards the faithful with cities to rule and takes the pound from the servant who hid it. Then Jesus goes on ahead, going up to Jerusalem.

scripture.text: And he said to him, 'Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.'
'I tell you, that to every one who has will more be given; but from him who has not, even what he has will be taken away.

art.title: The Entrusted Pounds (relief)
art.medium: Stone relief (photograph)
art.description: A crowned nobleman strides away with outstretched arm while his servants stand in a block holding golden coins; one figure apart clutches a single coin.
art.significance: A modern public relief on the parable, one of the Wege zur Kunst (Paths to Art) works in Schwäbisch Gmünd.
art.symbolism: The crown recalls that the nobleman goes away to receive a kingdom, the point Luke's version adds to the story.
art.impact: Shows how the parable still speaks in modern public art.
art.credit: Photo: Pedemann, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

events.orderNote: Robertson distinguishes this from the parable of the talents told a few days later (Matthew 25:14–30, §139); here the point is to check the crowd's hope of an immediate kingdom. Many readers hear an echo of Archelaus, who went to Rome in 4 BC to be confirmed as king while a Jewish embassy opposed him (Josephus, Antiquities 17).
